We present early James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) observations of 11 optically faint, infrared-bright galaxies at redshifts $z\sim 1-3$, selected from the Hubble Ultra Deep Field (HUDF) and HUDF09. These sources were identified as optically dim within the Hubble Ultra Deep Survey (HUDS) but detected in the Infrared Array Camera (IRAC) data. Our analysis reveals that these galaxies are predominantly star-forming systems with stellar masses ($M_\star$) ranging from $10^8$ to $10^{10} M_\odot$. The HUDF galaxies exhibit a median infrared luminosity ($L_{IR}$) approximately 100 times greater than that of HUDS galaxies at the same redshift, while their median optical luminosity ($L_{opt}$) is roughly 100 times fainter. This significant disparity in infrared brightness is primarily driven by a factor of 100 difference in star formation rates (SFR). Furthermore, the galaxies show a strong correlation between $L_{IR}$ and $L_{opt}$, with a slope of 1.1, indicating that their emission is dominated by the stellar population. The median ratio of infrared luminosity to star formation rate is $10^{44}$ erg/s per $M_\odot$ yr$^{-1}$, consistent with the standard Kennicutt-Robertson calibration. These findings suggest that the galaxies are viewed at a small angle relative to their star-forming disk plane, causing the optical light to be obscured by dust. This study demonstrates that the HUDF contains a substantial number of optically obscured, star-forming galaxies that were previously undetected. The discovery of these hidden galaxies in the HUDF and HUDF09 underscores the critical need for infrared observations to fully explore the star-forming history of the early universe. Our results also highlight the necessity of conducting deep, wide-field HUDS-like surveys in the infrared to uncover the true nature of the early universe. Finally, we demonstrate that the HUDF and HUDF09 are ideal targets for JWST, offering the potential to reveal the true star-forming history of the early universe. This study examines the global spatial patterns of seasonal precipitation extremes, specifically very low and high values, within the context of the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO). By analyzing the differential impacts of the three primary ENSO types—El Niño, La Niña, and neutral conditions—on these precipitation extremes, we identify distinct spatial patterns. The research utilizes a dataset of 1,000 gridded monthly precipitation records spanning 1950 to 2019, covering 110 countries and regions. We define the three ENSO types based on the standardized Niño-3.4 index, categorizing them as neutral (N), El Niño (EN), and La Niña (LN) when the index falls within [-0.5, 0.5], exceeds 0.5, and falls below -0.5, respectively. The analysis employs a 5-year moving window to calculate the 5-year mean precipitation for each year, followed by a 3-year moving window to determine the 3-year mean. Years are classified as wet or dry if the 3-year mean surpasses or falls below the 5-year mean, respectively. Furthermore, years are designated as extreme if the 3-year mean is at least 10% higher or lower than the 5-year mean. The study compares the spatial patterns of very low and elevated precipitation across the three ENSO types, revealing that the three types exhibit distinct spatial patterns for very low precipitation, whereas their patterns for elevated precipitation are more similar. Additionally, the spatial patterns of very low precipitation under El Niño and La Niña conditions are largely opposite. Finally, the spatial patterns of very low precipitation under El Niño and La Niña conditions are compared with those of very low temperature, indicating that the two types display similar spatial patterns for very low temperature. These findings offer valuable insights into the spatial distribution of precipitation extremes under different ENSO types, thereby enhancing our understanding of the mechanisms driving precipitation extremes globally. This knowledge is crucial for improving regional and local predictions of precipitation extremes under varying ENSO conditions. Finally, the results can assist in the development of regional and local early warning systems for precipitation extremes. We examine the evolution of non-affine growth in a two-dimensional model where particles are added to the surface of a square lattice, resulting in a flat geometry with four-fold symmetry. This growth process is driven by the non-affine vector connecting corresponding points on successive surfaces. By analyzing the distribution of this vector's magnitude and orientation, we observe that the resulting surface exhibits anisotropic self-affine roughness. This conclusion is supported by examining the surface power spectral density (PSD) across both real and reciprocal spaces. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the surface width scales with height according to a power law, where the exponent is determined by the surface roughness. Finally, we explore the potential for extending this model to more complex geometries. These findings are derived from extensive numerical simulations and confirmed by experimental data from vapor deposition on square lattices. Additionally, we compare our results with the well-known random sequential adsorption model. Our analysis indicates that the non-affine growth model is more general, as it encompasses both the random sequential adsorption model and the deposition on square lattices. We conclude that the non-affine growth model offers a versatile framework for studying surface roughness in various contexts. This work is dedicated to the memory of Professor J. M. López. This study addresses a stochastic job-shop scheduling problem characterized by non-deterministic ambiguity, where processing times are represented as discrete probability distributions. A key contribution is the introduction of a novel ambiguity modeling approach grounded in Monte Carlo simulation, which enables the estimation of the cumulative distribution function (CDF) for makespan. The paper demonstrates the application of this new method through two case studies, contrasting it with an existing technique derived from fuzzy set theory. Results indicate that the proposed simulation-based method outperforms the previous approach, offering greater flexibility and enhanced accuracy in predicting makespan distributions. Furthermore, the study explores the application of robust scheduling to manage this type of non-deterministic ambiguity. Ultimately, the research confirms the significant advantages of simulation-based methods for modeling non-deterministic data in job-shop environments. Finally, the paper discusses the broader applicability of the proposed methodology to other stochastic scheduling problems involving non-deterministic processing times.

Keywords: stochastic scheduling, non-deterministic data, discrete probability distributions, cumulative distribution function, robust scheduling.

This paper introduces a new robustness metric for cyber-physical systems (CPS) grounded in Signal Temporal Logic (STL). STL is particularly well-suited for specifying temporal properties of CPS, such as safety, liveness, and reachability. Our proposed metric quantifies robustness by evaluating the margin of a property's satisfaction. We demonstrate that this formulation offers several key benefits: first, the margin provides a precise measure of robustness that aligns with both human intuition and established engineering practices; second, it enables the ranking of multiple STL formulations to identify the most robust specification for a specific system; and third, it facilitates the analysis of how system parameters influence robustness. The effectiveness of this metric is validated through two case studies. The first examines a robotic arm's safety zone, where the margin represents the distance between the arm's tip and the zone's boundary. The second assesses the robustness of a controller for a second-order system, illustrating how the chosen STL formulation impacts the resulting margin. Finally, we introduce an algorithm that efficiently calculates this margin for STL formulas involving bounded quantifiers. Our approach is proven to be sound and complete, with its efficiency validated through extensive numerical experiments. Overall, our work establishes a novel framework for analyzing the robustness of CPS, offering a valuable tool for system designers. By quantifying robustness, designers can determine the extent to which a system can withstand disturbances and perturbations, thereby guiding decisions on whether to incorporate additional safety mechanisms or to select appropriate STL formulations for a given application. Furthermore, this framework supports the optimization of system parameters to achieve desired robustness levels. The framework is implemented in a Python library, which is available online.

Keywords: Cyber-Physical Systems, Signal Temporal Logic, Robustness, Bounded Quantifiers, Parameter Optimization.

Markov models serve as a mathematical framework for modeling stochastic processes, while quantitative information flow (QIF) measures the risk of information leakage within these models. This paper introduces a novel category of Markov models termed "concealed Markov models" (CMMs), which are derived from {\em quantitative information flow concealed Markov models} (QIF-CMMs). These structures are designed to represent the flow of information between inputs and outputs in stochastic processes. We demonstrate that both CMMs and QIF-CMMs can be defined as algebras for specific endofunctors on the category of sets. Furthermore, we show that these algebras possess a monadic structure, enabling the construction of a functor from sets to {\em commutative algebras} that preserves colimits. This monadic structure is leveraged to define the amount of information revealed by a given Markov model, providing a new, more concise, and conceptually distinct approach to QIF. This monadic framework for QIF is grounded in the theory of probabilistic computation, which utilizes monads to model probabilistic effects within programming languages. We illustrate the utility of this approach by applying it to two established metrics for measuring information flow in probabilistic programs. Finally, we outline a potential future direction for this research: the development of a probabilistic programming language that incorporates a stochastic process as a primitive data type. Such a language would enable the modeling of concealed Markov models and the calculation of their information flow using probabilistic programs. This proposal is motivated by the observation that probabilistic programs can be viewed as concealed Markov models, where the program itself functions as the transition matrix. Consequently, this work offers a fresh perspective on quantitative information flow, with a specific focus on probabilistic computation. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 reviews the foundational concepts of Markov models and quantitative information flow. Section 3 presents concealed Markov models and their algebraic structure. Section 4 details the monadic structure of these algebras and its application to a measure of information flow. Section 5 connects this monadic structure to probabilistic computation. Section 6 proposes a future research direction centered on probabilistic computation. The paper concludes with an outline of potential future work. Additionally, Section 7 provides a review of Markov models and quantitative information flow. We present a framework for analyzing the statistical nonlocality of coherent dynamical patterns, which quantifies the effective interaction range within a spatially extended system. This approach is applied to a globally coupled map model that exhibits both coherent and incoherent spatio-temporal patterns. Our results demonstrate that the statistical nonlocality of the coherent pattern is substantially greater than that of the incoherent pattern. Furthermore, we find that the transition from incoherence to coherence involves an increase in statistical nonlocality, a phenomenon that can be understood as the emergence of long-range correlations. These findings underscore the utility of our approach for investigating the formation of coherent structures in spatially extended systems. Additionally, we show that our definition of statistical nonlocality is equivalent to the participation ratio, a metric widely used in quantum physics. This equivalence enables the application of our framework to study the formation of Bose-Einstein condensates in spatially extended Bose gases. Finally, we discuss the broader implications of these results for physics. We introduce a phenomenological framework designed to investigate flexible scattering amplitudes across all kinematic regimes. This approach is grounded in the analytic properties of these amplitudes and their expansion within the soft limit. By applying this formalism to various processes involving quarks, gluons, and electroweak bosons, we derive constraints on the subleading soft functions governing these expanded terms. Furthermore, we demonstrate how this method can be extended to final-state observables, such as jet functions, and to particles with non-zero mass. Finally, we outline the application of this formalism to final-state soft radiation. Our findings are derived using the Berends-Dixon algorithm, though we also provide a brief outline of the adaptation required when employing the next-to-leading logarithmic (NLLx) algorithm. Additionally, we present numerical results for final-state soft radiation, comparing our outcomes with those from parton shower algorithms. This work serves as a precursor to a subsequent study where we develop a numerical implementation of the approach to construct flexible scattering cross sections. We introduce a new Point Cloud-based Global Localization method that leverages the Normal Distribution Transform (NDT). This approach utilizes a transformer-based architecture to identify the optimal NDT transformation parameters by processing point clouds as sequences of NDT cells. Our model is trained on a large-scale dataset comprising over 100,000 queries paired with 10,000 maps, covering both indoor and outdoor environments. Experimental results demonstrate that our method surpasses state-of-the-art techniques, achieving an average localization error of 0.11 meters across the entire dataset. Furthermore, we show that our model can be deployed on a Jetson Xavier NX for real-time inference, maintaining accuracy while operating at 15 frames per second. Resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI) connectivity is a widely used approach for characterizing brain networks and diagnosing neurological conditions. However, the reliability of rs-fMRI data is compromised by inherent noise, which can lead to inaccurate predictions of disease states. This study investigates the impact of noise on the statistical significance of connectivity findings and prediction accuracy. We developed a method to simulate noise in rs-fMRI data and applied it to resting-state fMRI scans from 100 healthy individuals. Our results indicate that noise can diminish statistical significance by up to 50% and reduce accuracy by as much as 60%. Furthermore, we introduced a new metric to evaluate the robustness of connectivity results against noise. This metric demonstrates a strong correlation with both the stability of connectivity and prediction accuracy, offering a valuable tool for assessing the reliability of rs-fMRI connectivity. These insights can guide researchers in selecting appropriate preprocessing and analysis techniques to mitigate noise effects. Additionally, we propose a novel method for estimating the signal-to-noise ratio in rs-fMRI data, which can be utilized to determine the necessary sample size for achieving a desired level of statistical significance. This work provides a framework for evaluating the robustness of rs-fMRI findings and offers a pathway for estimating the data volume required for significant statistical outcomes. The objective is to minimize total beeping activity while ensuring that nodes can identify one another. We establish that, for UIDs within the range [1, n], a node must beep at least $\log n - 1.5$ times on average to achieve identification. Furthermore, we present a deterministic algorithm that meets this lower bound, thereby resolving the identification problem with an optimal average beeping cost. Additionally, we address a variant where UIDs are drawn from an unknown distribution, deriving corresponding lower and upper bounds for this scenario. Our findings demonstrate that, provided the average UID is sufficiently large, the optimal average beeping cost approaches $\log n - 1.5$. This result contrasts with the case where UIDs are known to be drawn from a uniform distribution, which requires $\log n - 0.5$ beeps on average. We also explore extensions of these results to other graph topologies. Finally, our methodology yields a novel, simple proof for a previously established lower bound regarding energy-efficient naming using beeping. Our results indicate that this bound is tight for UIDs up to $n^2$, whereas the best existing lower bound was previously limited to $n^3$. Code-mixed (CM) languages are a prevalent linguistic phenomenon, yet current pre-trained language models (PLMs) struggle to effectively leverage their statistical patterns due to the inherent code-switching. This paper introduces PESTO, a transformer-based framework designed to capture the transitional dynamics of code-mixing through a novel dynamic and relative positional encoding method. This study employs first-principles calculations to analyze the pressure-dependent isotope effect on the critical temperature ($T_c$) for H$_3$S hydride. By employing the first-principles Eliashberg formalism, we compute the pressure-induced isotope effect on $T_c$ across a broad range of electron-phonon coupling strengths ($\lambda$). Our findings indicate that at high pressures, the isotope effect on $T_c$ diminishes due to the presence of a van Hove singularity in the phonon density of states. Furthermore, we observe that the isotope effect on $T_c$ is more pronounced at lower pressures, where the electron-phonon coupling strength is weaker. These results offer valuable insights into the pressure-dependent isotope influence on the superconducting transition temperature of H$_3$S. Additionally, our calculated $T_c$ values align well with experimental data. Finally, we demonstrate that the first-principles Eliashberg method accurately predicts the isotope effect on $T_c$ for H$_3$S hydride superconductor. These outcomes underscore the efficacy of the first-principles Eliashberg approach in investigating the isotope effect on $T_c$ within high-temperature superconductors. We demonstrate that a sequence of uniformly continuous, irreducible Markov chains on a countable state space, characterized by progressively diminishing probabilities of positive cycles, consistently and convergently approaches the Q-process. Furthermore, we establish that the associated exit times from open subsets of the state space, which are finite with probability one, exhibit uniform integrability. These findings are applied to various q-absorbing processes, including those derived from uniformly hyperbolic dynamical systems and those originating from uniformly contracting Markov processes on locally compact spaces. The latter application yields a significant result: the finiteness of the expected lifetime for a uniformly q-absorbing process on a countable state space is a necessary condition for the existence of a non-trivial solution to the associated Yaglom problem. Additionally, we generalize the concept of uniform contraction to locally compact spaces and provide a criterion for uniform contraction based on the existence of a Lyapunov function. Finally, we illustrate the application of our results to uniformly q-absorbing processes on the real line through examples involving the Gauss map, the tent map, and the map $x\mapsto 2x^2-1$. In each instance, we construct a specific solution to the Yaglom problem. Notably, for the case involving the Gauss map, this constitutes the first example of a uniformly q-absorbing process on a countable state space where the existence of a non-trivial solution to the Yaglom problem does not imply uniform contraction. This work extends the results of [10] and [11] to the setting of uniformly q-absorbing processes. The primary tool employed is the construction of a family of invariant measures for the approximating Markov chains, which is derived from the existence of a Lyapunov function. We also provide a criterion for the existence of such a Lyapunov function applicable to a broad class of Markov chains. Finally, we introduce a novel application of our findings to the study of q-absorbing processes on the real line, specifically addressing the existence of invariant measures for these processes. This work expands upon the results of [12]. Finally, we examine the implications of our findings for the theory of q-absorbing Markov processes. In this context, we define a q-absorbing process as one where the probability of absorption in a finite number of steps is zero, and we define uniform contraction as the condition where the rate of absorption in a finite number of steps converges to zero as the q-parameter approaches zero

Two Higgs doublet models (2HDM) are a popular extension of the Standard Model (SM) that can account for various flavor anomalies and potentially explain the Higgs boson mass. This paper examines the compatibility of the most general 2HDM with recent LHC measurements of the SM-like Higgs boson, as well as with current constraints from B-physics and low-energy flavor experiments. We demonstrate that while the SM-compatible region exists within the 2HDM, it is severely restricted by low-energy flavor data. Furthermore, we analyze the prospects for discovering the additional two Higgs bosons at the HL-LHC and the future FCC-ee and FCC-hh. Our findings indicate that the HL-LHC may only marginally improve the exclusion limits for the SM-compatible region, whereas both FCC-ee and FCC-hh could significantly enhance these exclusion capabilities. Additionally, we show that the FCC-ee and FCC-hh have the potential to directly discover the 2HDM parameter space capable of addressing B-physics anomalies. These results underscore the critical importance of low-energy flavor experiments in probing the 2HDM parameter space. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for the design and prioritization of future collider facilities. This study serves as a comprehensive guide for phenomenologists investigating the 2HDM. Our conclusions are based on a global fit incorporating all available data, including recent LHC Higgs measurements, B-physics, and low-energy flavor experiments. We have also included a Python code that performs this fit and can be easily updated with future experimental results. This code is publicly accessible and will be valuable for researchers studying the 2HDM. We conclude that the 2HDM is a viable framework for explaining various flavor anomalies, and that future collider experiments will play a pivotal role in exploring this parameter space. This paper examines the steady Navier-Stokes equations within the critical Besov space $B^0_{\infty,1}$. We demonstrate that there exists a specific class of divergence-free initial data for which no steady solution exists. Furthermore, we establish that this ill-posedness remains invariant under rotations of the initial conditions. These findings are derived through an analysis of the linearized problem and the application of the maximum principle. Additionally, we prove that for any divergence-free initial condition, a steady solution may exist within a lower regularity space characterized by a negative smoothness index. Finally, we address the possibility of constructing counterexamples using the profile decomposition method. The techniques employed here are anticipated to be applicable to other linearized systems in fluid dynamics. As an illustration, we provide a counterexample for the steady Euler equations in three dimensions. Finally, we offer a concise overview of recent advancements regarding the ill-posedness of the steady Navier-Stokes equations in critical spaces. These results are expected to have significant implications for the understanding of the Navier-Stokes equations. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 presents preliminary results and notations; Section 3 proves the main theorem; Section 4 provides an example of the profile decomposition; and Section 5 concludes with remarks and a discussion of related problems. This study investigates the nonlinear dynamics of thermal magnons within antiferromagnetic insulators. By applying a canonical ensemble to a minimal two-sublattice model, we derive a nonlinear equation of motion for the magnon amplitude that includes a thermal damping term and a nonlinear compression force. The latter arises from the interaction between the magnon amplitude and the sublattice antiferromagnetic order parameter, which is treated as a slowly varying background. The thermal magnon frequency is calculated perturbatively, revealing a nonlinear thermal compression force that intensifies with temperature. This effect stems from the temperature-dependent free energy of the magnon amplitude. Additionally, we identify a nonlinear spectral displacement caused by the interaction between the magnon amplitude and the thermal reservoir. This displacement is proportional to the temperature and the square of the driving field amplitude. We further examine the conditions under which this nonlinear compression force can be observed experimentally. Finally, we compare our theoretical findings with the previously proposed semiclassical model. The proposed model is validated through a comparison with the equation of motion derived from a quantum model. We conclude that the quantum model accurately describes the behavior of a thermal nonlinear oscillator in an antiferromagnetic insulator. Our results demonstrate that magnons in antiferromagnetic insulators exhibit unique quantum properties, including quantum fluctuations and entanglement, which can be harnessed for quantum information processing. The proposed model offers a framework for investigating these quantum effects and for developing new applications in magnonics. Specifically, the model can be utilized to design devices that manipulate magnons using nonlinear forces, such as compressors and expanders. Additionally, the model can serve as a basis for studying the interaction between magnons and other quasiparticles, such as phonons and photons. The findings of this work have significant implications for the development of antiferromagnetic insulators as promising materials for magnon-based technologies. The proposed model provides a foundation for exploring the quantum properties of magnons in these materials and for advancing new applications in magnonics. Furthermore, the results of this work may have broader implications for the study of nonlinear dynamics in other condensed matter systems. The proposed model can be extended to investigate the behavior of thermal excitations in other magnetic materials, such as ferrimagnets and ferromagnets. Additionally, the findings of this work may have relevance for the study of nonlinear dynamics in other systems, such as optical and mechanical systems. The proposed model can be adapted to investigate the behavior of thermal excitations in these systems, thereby expanding the scope of magnon-based technologies.

We establish bounds for the expected values of limiting minimal spanning acycles and limiting persistence diagrams within random simplicial complexes. Specifically, for a random complex defined by a threshold function $p_p(n)$, we demonstrate that the limiting minimal spanning acycle for the $k$-cycles of a random $d$-uniform hypergraph is bounded above by $O\left(\frac{n^{k+1}}{p_p(n)}\right)$. This result holds for $k$-cycles where $k \geq 2$, encompassing both 2-cycles (edges) and 3-cycles (faces). Additionally, we prove a corresponding bound for the limiting persistence diagram of the 2-dimensional homology of a random triangle mesh. Furthermore, we derive an upper bound for the limiting minimal spanning tree in a random graph where the edge probability is given by $p_p(n) = \frac{c \ln n}{n}$. In this scenario, the resulting bound is $O\left(\frac{n}{p_p(n)}\right)$. These findings are derived by integrating results from random graph theory with the framework of random complexes. Our work extends the methodology introduced by Bader et al. [2019], which utilized limiting minimal spanning trees in random graphs to bound the limiting persistence diagrams of random triangle meshes. Our approach employs a similar strategy but incorporates more refined probabilistic tools to achieve tighter bounds. We anticipate that these results will facilitate the analysis of large-scale geometric data structures, such as Delaunay triangulations, point cloud reconstructions, and mesh generation. Finally, we propose that the bounds presented herein may be applicable to other random graph properties, including limiting chromatic numbers and the size of the largest independent sets.

Vertical Federated Learning (VFL) represents a privacy-centric framework where multiple parties collaborate to train machine learning models by contributing only their local feature data. This paper introduces two novel practical attacks targeting VFL systems, designed to breach user privacy by reconstructing missing feature values. Our approach leverages a feature engineering technique to generate synthetic features that mimic the characteristics of missing ones, thereby enhancing attack efficacy. We validate the utility of these synthesized features across various VFL configurations. The proposed attack achieves a 10% to 20% increase in feature reconstruction accuracy compared to current state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the attack remains effective even when model performance is optimized, challenging the common assumption that VFL inherently safeguards user privacy. These findings underscore the urgent need for additional privacy-preserving strategies within VFL frameworks. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ashishkumar12345/PragmaticPrivacyAssaultsOnVFL. This work was presented at the 28th USENIX Security Symposium (USENIX Security 2019).

This expression relies on the proton's distribution amplitudes and the $B$ meson's light-cone distribution amplitude. This paper introduces a new intelligent city defense framework designed to counter coordinated assaults on Socio-Cyber-Physical (SCP) systems. The core concept involves a city-wide game engine that dynamically simulates the evolution of an ongoing attack, utilizing a novel scoring system to evaluate the effectiveness of various defensive strategies. This game engine is integrated with a tactical decision support system that offers real-time recommendations to defense operators, enabling them to allocate resources optimally and adapt to the dynamic nature of the assault. This paper examines a singular curvature flow where crystals evolve by their crystalline-like average curvature. We provide an overview of the short-time existence, non-existence of boundary oscillations, and the long-time existence and convergence of the flow. Additionally, we investigate the convergence of polyhedra and tetrahedra under this flow. The analysis of polyhedra is restricted to the case where the crystalline-like surface tension function is piecewise quadratic. Finally, we demonstrate that the flow preserves the crystalline nature of the initial geometry. Furthermore, we establish that the flow maintains the face structure of a tetrahedron during evolution, thereby enabling the derivation of asymptotic and convergence results for this specific shape. All proofs are presented in a self-contained manner. Finally, we explore potential applications of these findings to the study of the anisotropic singular mean curvature flow of a torus.

Plants are vital to human survival, yet they are highly sensitive to environmental factors, making it difficult to cultivate them in optimal conditions. Although environmental control systems exist, they often rely on manual tuning or reinforcement learning, both of which are time-consuming and demand significant human expertise. To address these challenges, we introduce GrowSpace, a system designed to automatically learn how to adjust an environment for plant growth. GrowSpace utilizes an online learning algorithm that continuously refines an action-value function based on real-time plant responses. This approach enables the system to adaptively tune environmental parameters to maximize growth for specific plant varieties. We validated GrowSpace by applying it to control an indoor garden, demonstrating that it can successfully identify and implement environmental settings that optimize plant growth. Our results indicate that GrowSpace can achieve growth rates comparable to those achieved by human experts. Furthermore, we show that the system can generalize its learning to varieties not previously exposed to its adjustments. GrowSpace offers a promising framework for automating environmental control in agricultural settings. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/andrewgao10/growspace.

This study introduces a method for detecting mechanically generated headlines by leveraging syntactic and semantic features. We fine-tune a pre-trained Transformer model to extract these features, which are then fed into a support vector machine classifier. Calibration is a critical phase in radio interferometry, where the performance of various algorithms is evaluated based on their computational efficiency and signal recovery capabilities. The results indicate that the proposed approach is at least as effective as current techniques while offering superior computational efficiency. Furthermore, the method is highly scalable, successfully handling up to $10^6$ baselines on a single CPU core. The source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/abhishekgupta1997/FFTcal. We introduce a novel autoencoding conditional Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) designed to create diversified portfolios. This approach leverages the inherent generative capabilities of conditional GANs to produce synthetic data that captures the underlying structure of the input. This paper introduces two tensor product operations for hypergraphs and investigates their spectral properties. Specifically, we establish sufficient conditions regarding the eigenvalues of a hypergraph that guarantee sufficient connectivity. Additionally, we demonstrate that these operations induce equivalent operations on the corresponding adjacency tensors. Finally, we explore the implications of these tensor products for functionals defined on hypergraphs. A primary motivation for this research is the desire to extend established graph theory concepts into the domain of hypergraphs. While various definitions of tensor products for hypergraphs exist in the literature, they often lack desirable characteristics; therefore, our approach aims to address these limitations. Furthermore, we examine the relationship between eigenvalues and connectivity within hypergraphs, a topic that has received limited attention in existing studies. Our findings indicate that eigenvalues can effectively quantify connectivity in hypergraphs. The paper concludes by outlining several open questions for future research. To support these results, we have also developed a software package for computing hypergraph tensor products, which is available at \url{https://github.com/abhishekgupta1997/HypergraphTensorProducts}. This study investigates natural cubic splines for analyzing Alzheimer's disease clinical trials. We propose a regression model where the natural cubic spline serves as the link function for a Poisson regression, with the spline's coefficients representing the treatment effects. To address the selection of the optimal number of knots, we employ a Bayesian information criterion (BIC) that incorporates a penalty term for the complexity of the treatment effect. This penalty term is derived from the expected number of changes in the treatment effect's sign across various knot locations. Additionally, we examine a model selection procedure that integrates this knot selection method with a model averaging approach. Through simulation studies, we demonstrate that this model selection procedure outperforms alternatives in terms of accuracy and computational efficiency. Finally, we apply the proposed method to data from a randomized clinical trial evaluating the efficacy of donepezil for Alzheimer's disease. The resulting estimates and confidence intervals indicate that donepezil has a statistically significant impact on the outcome variable. Furthermore, we observe that the treatment effect is positive at lower levels of the outcome but becomes negative at higher levels. These findings align with previous research suggesting that donepezil may be more effective in mild to moderate Alzheimer's cases compared to severe ones. We introduce a new global optimization technique for identifying action-minimizing paths between specified states in dissipative stochastic dynamics. This approach, known as the "optimal path method," is demonstrated using a two-dimensional double-well potential featuring asymmetric escape rates and varying friction levels. The study highlights the method's efficiency in mapping the phase space of escape trajectories and pinpointing the most probable transition routes. Furthermore, the optimal path method is shown to be broadly applicable across diverse stochastic dynamics. Its implementation relies on a straightforward numerical algorithm that employs a novel cost function to identify the system's most probable transition paths. By integrating this cost function with a genetic algorithm, the method successfully and rapidly converges to the global minimum of the quasi-potential, even within high-dimensional systems. These findings indicate that the proposed global optimization method serves as a versatile tool for analyzing escape dynamics in both simple and complex systems. The associated software is accessible at https://github.com/akimura-lab/optimal_path_method. The source code for all simulations presented in this work can be found at https://github.com/akimura-lab/OPTPATH2D.

This paper investigates the connection between a class of functions on $\mathbb{N}^k$ and a specific typed lambda-calculus. The function class encompasses all functions computable by regular circuits, including De Morgan functions, and is defined by the existence of a finite set of functions $\mathcal{F}$ such that every function in the class is composed of functions from $\mathcal{F}$ using only constant functions and projections. We demonstrate that the typed lambda-calculus, when augmented with constants from the finite set $\mathcal{F}$, precisely characterizes this class of functions. Finally, we outline an extension of this characterization to include functions computable by constant-size circuits with a linear number of gates. This study addresses the challenge of mapping natural language to SQL queries within a cross-domain context. We introduce a novel end-to-end framework that utilizes an auxiliary task to facilitate structural analysis. Our approach integrates an Auxiliary Structure Alignment Layer (ASAL) into a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network, enabling the model to identify and align structural elements in both input sentences. By incorporating this auxiliary alignment task into the primary task objective, we enhance the model's capacity to leverage structural information for SQL generation. Experimental results demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on both the Spider and ConceptualSQL datasets. Furthermore, we analyze the ASAL's ability to extract structural data and explore its impact on the primary task outcomes. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi-1997/SQL_generation.

This paper introduces a new Information-Focused Risk-Aware Model Predictive Control (IFFR-MPC) framework designed for secure navigation in multi-robot systems. The approach prioritizes the safe delivery of specific robots while optimizing the performance of others. To achieve this, the study first defines a novel information metric that quantifies the uncertainty regarding a robot's ability to reach its destination safely. Subsequently, this metric is integrated into a two-stage optimization process: the first stage generates a safe reference trajectory by minimizing uncertainty, and the second stage executes a risk-aware MPC to track that reference while ensuring probabilistic safety constraints are met. The paper presents a computationally efficient algorithm to solve the resulting non-convex optimization problem. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed framework significantly reduces the uncertainty of the target robot's safe arrival and enhances the overall performance of the multi-robot system. Finally, experimental data from a real-world multi-robot navigation scenario validate the effectiveness of the proposed approach. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi2000/IFFR-MPC. We report the discovery of Andromeda XXV (And XXV), a compact dwarf galaxy situated approximately 780 kiloparsecs from Earth. This object was identified through a deep survey of the Andromeda galaxy's halo conducted with the VLT Survey Telescope (VST) at ESO's La Silla Observatory. We determined its heliocentric radial velocity to be $v_{\rm helio} = 202 \pm 1$ km/s. By analyzing its color and luminosity, we classified it as an ultra-faint dwarf galaxy. Our study of its stellar population indicates an age of $10.5 \pm 0.5$ billion years and a metallicity of $[Fe/H] = -1.7 \pm 0.2$ dex. Furthermore, we determined its distance to be $780 \pm 10$ kiloparsecs, yielding a physical half-light radius of $1.0 \pm 0.1$ parsecs. The galaxy's total mass within this radius is estimated at $M_{1/2} = 1.1 \pm 0.1 \times 10^7 M_{\odot}$, resulting in a mass-to-light ratio of $\Upsilon_{1/2} = 1000 \pm 100 M_{\odot}/L_{\odot}$. These findings suggest that And XXV is a dark matter-dominated dwarf galaxy. Additionally, we observed that And XXV is likely on a highly eccentric orbit around the Andromeda galaxy. Finally, we discuss the implications of these results for the formation and evolution of dwarf galaxies within the Andromeda system. Non-orthogonal sequences are essential for grant-free massive connectivity, where a large number of devices share a short sequence pool to transmit data without requesting sequence assignments. This paper introduces a two-stage genetic algorithm designed to create non-orthogonal sequences that minimize Hamming distances between pairs. The first stage generates sequences with constant amplitude and zero auto-correlation side-lobes using a modified genetic approach. The second stage utilizes the outputs from the first stage as an initial population to further reduce Hamming distances. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed sequences achieve lower Hamming distances compared to existing methods, thereby enhancing system performance. Additionally, the algorithm's computational complexity is significantly lower than that of other related techniques. Finally, the study examines the impact of sequence design on grant-free massive connectivity, showing that the proposed sequences improve system performance relative to other sequence designs. The source code is accessible at \url{https://github.com/ahmedhassan1997/Two-Stage-Genetic-Algorithm}. The corresponding manuscript can be found at \url{https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.07009}. This study examines various approximations for modeling humid air, focusing on their thermodynamic and mathematical characteristics. The analysis begins by defining the thermodynamic framework for moist air and deriving the fundamental equations governing its behavior. Subsequently, the paper evaluates the thermodynamic coherence of several commonly employed approximations, including the ideal gas law, the saturation vapor pressure curve, and the saturation ratio. Finally, a systematic approach is introduced for constructing thermodynamically coherent approximations, which are then applied to specific instances. The resulting models are designed to facilitate the development of accurate yet computationally efficient models for both dry and moist air. Finally, the practical applications of these thermodynamically consistent approximations are demonstrated. The proposed models are intended for use in both theoretical and computational fluid dynamics simulations. Additionally, the authors intend to utilize these models in future research concerning the development of a new numerical framework for simulating moist convection. This framework will be based on the anelastic approximation and will incorporate a thermodynamically coherent moist convection model. The authors will release the resulting code under an open-source license. Furthermore, the authors will publish a follow-up paper detailing the theoretical and computational aspects of this new framework. The current paper will be utilized as a reference for that subsequent publication. Finally, the authors acknowledge that this work was conducted independently of any funding sources. In abstract convexity spaces, the concept of an "outer" element—defined as one not belonging to any hyperplane relative to a given set—has been established. This paper extends the theory of outer elements to matroid theory. We demonstrate that for any set $A$ within a matroid $M$, there exists a specific subset $B \subseteq A$ such that every element of $A$ is "outer" with respect to $B$. Additionally, we explore the relationship between outer elements and antichains in matroids. Furthermore, we establish an analogue of the Erdős-Ko-Rado theorem specifically for outer elements in matroids. Finally, we introduce the notion of "strongly outer" elements and provide a characterization of this concept for matroids derived from directed graphs. As an application, we derive a characterization of the strongly connected components in a directed graph. The paper concludes with an examination of the NP-hardness of identifying maximal outer elements in matroids. We introduce a new method for training dialogue state tracking (DST) models that incorporates ASR uncertainty. To model this uncertainty, we utilize word confusion networks (WCN) as a compact representation of the full probability distribution across the ASR output space. By integrating the WCN into a single transcription, we create an enhanced representation that captures word-level uncertainty. We demonstrate that this approach yields superior DST performance compared to using the most probable WCN path. Our experiments across two English dialogue datasets confirm the effectiveness of WCNs in modeling ASR uncertainty, with models trained on this data outperforming those trained on standard ASR transcriptions. Additionally, we present an analysis of the learned DST models to offer insights into their internal representations. The code is accessible at https://github.com/abhi-12345/ASR-uncertainty-for-DST. We introduce an efficient algorithm for computing global sections of line sheaves on curves within the computer algebra system Sage. This method is grounded in the exact triangle connecting line sheaves, their duals, and the resulting trace maps. The algorithm is implemented in computer algebra systems Sage and Macaulay2, with a recent integration into Sage version 9.2. We validate the implementation by comparing its outputs against established formulas for divisors on $\mathbb{P}^1$ and $\mathbb{P}^2$, as well as against the Riemann-Roch formula. Additionally, we utilize the software to investigate the geometry of moduli spaces of sheaves on curves. Specifically, we examine the moduli space of rank 2 sheaves on $\mathbb{P}^1$ with a fixed determinant, which corresponds to the space of binary forms of a specific degree modulo scaling. By calculating the cohomology of line sheaves on this space, we determine the Euler characteristics of the moduli space and the space of stable sheaves. Furthermore, we compute the cohomology of the tangent sheaf to derive the Euler characteristics for both the space of sheaves and the space of stable sheaves. Finally, we apply the Grothendieck-Riemann-Roch formula to calculate the class of the space of stable sheaves within the cohomology ring of the moduli space of binary forms. These computations align with previously published results. Additionally, we have developed a Sage package, `cohomology.sheaves`, to facilitate these computations. The package's documentation, including examples, is accessible at https://cohomology.sheaves.

We introduce a method to calculate intricacy for universal entry frameworks. First, we establish the concept of intricacy for these frameworks and demonstrate that it aligns with the intricacy of the underlying languages. Second, we prove that the intricacy of a universal entry framework remains invariant regardless of the specific set of target languages selected. Third, we derive an explicit formula for this invariant value. Finally, we apply these findings to the situations where the framework comprises all deterministic context-free languages and all context-free languages. As an application, we establish that the intricate encoding length is equivalent to the Sipp length for deterministic context-free languages and is bounded by the yield length for context-free languages. Additionally, we show that the intricate encoding length exceeds the yield length for certain context-free languages. Furthermore, we prove that the intricate encoding length surpasses both the Sipp length and the yield length for specific deterministic context-free languages. Finally, we provide an upper bound for the intricate encoding length of deterministic context-free languages using yield length. These findings represent the first instance of utilizing intricacy to investigate the relationships among various length measures associated with context-free languages. The techniques developed in this study are also applicable to other universal entry frameworks. We introduce a method for efficiently assessing entanglement within qubit systems by utilizing a single measurement configuration. This approach is applied to polarization-entangled photons generated via spontaneous parametric down-conversion, where we analyze the impact of decoherence on the source. The findings indicate that this technique is broadly applicable to optical qubit systems, offering potential for extension to higher-dimensional entangled states. Additionally, the proposed framework may prove valuable for quantum information processing tasks involving entanglement verification. Addressing Continual Learning (CL) remains a critical challenge in deep learning, where models must acquire new tasks without forgetting prior ones. While numerous methods have been proposed, many depend on extra capacity like parameter or replay buffers, which are often impractical for real-world applications. Although some approaches leverage pretrained models to mitigate catastrophic forgetting, their effectiveness in CL scenarios remains uncertain. This paper presents a straightforward baseline that challenges the application of pretrained models in this context. We demonstrate that our method matches or surpasses the performance of recent CL techniques on standard benchmarks, including CIFAR100, TinyImageNet, and TAU. Furthermore, we analyze the limitations of these models and explore their potential within CL frameworks. The code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi-1998/Straightforward-Baseline. This study examines how degree distribution heterogeneity influences the synchronization of type-I neurons connected via random synapses. We begin by deriving the mean-field equations governing the evolution of the order parameter, which characterizes synchronization, for both networks with homogeneous degrees and those featuring heterogeneous degrees. These equations are subsequently solved numerically. Our results indicate that networks with power-law degree distributions are more prone to synchronization than those with exponential degree distributions. Furthermore, we observe that the presence of hubs in networks with power-law degree distributions can induce synchronization even when the coupling strength is below the threshold required for synchronization in networks with homogeneous degrees. Finally, we demonstrate that the coexistence of multiple attractors is more likely to occur in networks with heterogeneous degrees than in those with homogeneous degrees. These findings are validated through numerical simulations of the FitzHugh-Nagumo model. Additionally, we show that these conclusions extend to networks of theta neurons, which also exhibit type-I dynamics. This research underscores the critical role of network structure in the synchronization of type-I neurons. These findings are particularly relevant for understanding the dynamics of heterogeneous neural populations, such as those found in the cerebral cortex. Moreover, they may offer insights into the mechanisms underlying the emergence of epileptic seizures. Finally, our results could contribute to a deeper understanding of the dynamics of coupled oscillators with heterogeneous frequencies. This is especially pertinent for investigating the dynamics of Josephson junctions, which are essential components in quantum computing. In this context, our findings may aid in the design of qubits and the development of quantum algorithms. To achieve this, it is crucial to understand how the heterogeneity of Josephson frequencies affects the dynamics of the system. Our results provide valuable insights into this issue. In conclusion, this work highlights the importance of network structure in the synchronization of type-I neurons and offers a foundation for further research into the dynamics of complex networks. This includes the study of other neuronal models, such as those exhibiting type-II dynamics, as well as the investigation of the effects of other factors, such as the presence of inhibitory neurons, on the dynamics of the system. This research could lead to a better understanding of the mechanisms underlying brain function and the development of new treatments for neurological disorders. In summary, this work provides a comprehensive understanding of the effects of network structure on the synchronization of type-I neurons and paves the way for future research in this area. This includes the study of other neuronal models, the effects of network structure on the dynamics of type-II neurons, and the role of network structure in the emergence of complex brain dynamics.

By leveraging these antagonistic pairs, we demonstrate that repair systems can more effectively locate and rectify defects. Our empirical findings indicate that incorporating this contextual data enhances both the accuracy and recall rates of program repair efforts. Furthermore, we have integrated this technique into Dr. Fixit, a leading automated repair tool, and our results show that it successfully repairs additional bugs compared to the baseline version. This study investigates the capability region of grouped independent and identically distributed full-duplex two-way channels. In this setup, two users exchange information over a shared wireless link, with each user capable of simultaneously transmitting and receiving full-duplex signals. The users employ grouped data spectrum processing to achieve a finite number of groups, where each group contains an infinite number of data dimensions. We demonstrate that the capability region of this channel is the convex hull formed by the union of the capability regions of all possible data spectrum processing schemes. Furthermore, we derive the capability region for a specific scenario involving time-varying channels. Finally, we compare the achievable rates using data spectrum processing against traditional time-division and frequency-division strategies. The findings indicate that the proposed data spectrum approach yields a significant performance gain compared to both time- and frequency-division methods. Additionally, the derived achievable rates are shown to be tight. The results also reveal that the achievable rate for each user is bounded from above by the minimum of the user's channel capacity and the sum-rate capability of the channel. These upper bounds are achieved when the number of data spectrum groups is sufficiently large. Finally, we examine the capability region for a specific instance of the channel and provide a numerical illustration of the performance gains. The paper concludes with a discussion on the potential application of data spectrum processing in other communication scenarios. We introduce a new method for analyzing three-dimensional flow in high-energy nuclear collisions, which simultaneously determines the collision geometry and the equation of state (EOS). This approach is validated using results from the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider (RHIC). The collision geometry is characterized by a three-dimensional ellipsoid, defined by its semi-axes, whereas the EOS is represented by the speed of sound. By applying Bayesian model analysis, we derive posterior probability distributions for these parameters. Our findings indicate that the collision geometry is highly sensitive to the impact parameter, while the speed of sound is significantly influenced by beam energy. Furthermore, we observe that the speed of sound varies with centrality, a phenomenon that can be accounted for by the energy dependence of the collision geometry. This technique offers a novel and complementary tool for investigating the EOS of nuclear matter. Additionally, we demonstrate that the posterior probability distributions for the ellipsoid's semi-axes align with those obtained through a Bayesian analysis of the three-dimensional participant anisotropy. Finally, we outline a strategy for enhancing the precision of ellipsoid parameters by incorporating additional observables. These results establish a foundation for future research into the EOS of nuclear matter. This work is based on research conducted at the Brookhaven National Laboratory. The ongoing COVID-19 pandemic has caused widespread disruption to daily life and global economies. While medical professionals have been on the front lines, they have faced significant challenges in diagnosing the disease due to the scarcity of testing resources. To address this, researchers have developed various non-invasive methods for early detection, including chest X-rays, CT scans, and cough audio analysis. However, these approaches often fail to account for the privacy risks inherent in data collection and usage. This paper introduces a novel framework for the early detection of COVID-19 that leverages adversarial training to mitigate privacy concerns. Our results demonstrate that this framework achieves state-of-the-art performance in both classification accuracy and robustness against membership inference attacks. Furthermore, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the trade-offs between accuracy and privacy within our model. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/raja-singh/privacy-covid19. To our knowledge, this is the first study to apply adversarial training to the task of detecting COVID-19 from cough audio. The experiments were conducted using the ESC-STS2017 dataset, which contains over 5,000 cough audio samples. The evaluation focused on distinguishing between healthy and COVID-19 patients. We assessed the model's performance against several state-of-the-art methods, including a baseline and other recent works, using metrics such as classification accuracy, F1 score, and AUC-ROC. Additionally, we evaluated the model's resilience to membership inference attacks, a critical aspect of model privacy. The results indicate that our proposed framework outperforms all compared methods in terms of accuracy and privacy protection. The source code can be found at https://github.com/raja-singh/privacy-covid19. The experiments utilized the ESC-STS2017 dataset, which includes more than 5,000 cough audio recordings. The analysis examined the balance between the model's performance and its privacy characteristics. The evaluation involved comparing our approach against multiple state-of-the-art techniques, including a baseline and other recent studies, with evaluation metrics encompassing classification accuracy, F1 score, and AUC-ROC. Moreover, the model's robustness against membership inference attacks was examined. The findings reveal that the proposed framework surpasses all compared methods in achieving superior accuracy and privacy preservation. The source code is available at https://github.com/raja-singh/privacy-covid19. The experiments were conducted using the ESC-STS2017 dataset

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have recently demonstrated exceptional performance in various wireless transmission systems, such as MIMO precoding and channel estimation, by leveraging the topological structure of signal graphs. However, the computational complexity of GNNs increases with the number of nodes, making centralized training and inference impractical for large-scale graphs. This paper introduces a distributed inference framework for GNNs that utilizes the communication architecture of wireless transmission systems. In this approach, training and inference are executed collaboratively by relays and user equipments (UEs) within a wireless network. Simulation results indicate that the proposed method achieves performance comparable to centralized implementations while significantly reducing computational complexity. Furthermore, this framework offers a promising pathway for the practical deployment of GNNs in real-world wireless transmission systems. Additionally, we outline potential future research directions concerning GNNs in wireless communications. Finally, we provide an open-source implementation of the proposed framework, available at \url{https://github.com/zhongyuanwang123/GNN-Distributed-Inference}. Homicide rates in Brazil have historically been high, with recent data indicating a surge in the early 2000s followed by a decline. This study analyzes the spatial distribution of homicides across the Brazilian province of Goiás between 2002 and 2014. By applying the Scan statistic, we identified the most affected municipalities within this region. Furthermore, we examined the correlation between homicide rates and the proportion of the population living in poverty. Our findings reveal that the municipalities with the highest homicide rates are concentrated in the most populous areas of the province, and that the relationship between homicide rates and poverty is stronger during periods of homicide reduction. Additionally, the study demonstrates that the Scan statistic is a valuable tool for identifying high-risk municipalities, which can inform future public policy initiatives. Finally, we propose a method for visualizing the results of the Scan statistic to facilitate the creation of an interactive map. This approach involves representing the study area as a graph, where nodes correspond to municipalities and edges denote adjacency; the resulting graph is then visualized using a force-directed algorithm. This visualization technique allows for the identification of high-risk municipalities and the detection of clusters within the study area. Accelerated stochastic gradient descent (Adam) is a widely adopted method for training deep neural networks. This paper introduces two enhancements to Adam: (1) a sound-adaptive variant that adjusts step sizes based on the magnitude of gradients, and (2) an issue-adaptive variant that adapts step sizes to the specific problems at hand. Both proposed methods are straightforward to implement and require no additional hyperparameters. We evaluate these approaches across various scenarios, including diverse deep learning tasks and random projections of high-dimensional data. Our results demonstrate that these simple modifications yield significant performance improvements over the original Adam algorithm. The Sun's core is a primary source of neutrinos and solar axions. While neutrino experiments have already confirmed the standard solar model, axion searches have yet to yield a detection. The upcoming space-based gamma-ray experiment BabyIAXO will investigate the solar interior by searching for solar axions. This study presents a comprehensive analysis of the expected sensitivity of BabyIAXO, detailing the primary and secondary factors influencing its performance. The analysis reveals a sensitivity of approximately $10^{-12}$ cm$^2$ at the peak of the PRL profile, which aligns with the predictions of the standard solar model. Furthermore, BabyIAXO is capable of constraining the axion coupling constant to a level of $10^{-11}$ cm$^2$, thereby significantly improving upon current limits. This research demonstrates that BabyIAXO will be able to probe the Sun's interior with unprecedented precision. Additionally, the study examines the potential for BabyIAXO to detect new physics beyond the standard model, including a light sterile neutrino, a dark photon, and a light scalar. The resulting constraints on these particles will advance our understanding of the solar interior. This work serves as a precursor to the upcoming BabyIAXO mission. This paper introduces a new class of self-exciting systems, extending beyond the well-known self-exciting threshold systems. The proposed model is analyzed using tools from variational calculus and dynamical systems theory. The study highlights key qualitative characteristics, including various equilibrium configurations and bifurcation structures. Furthermore, specific instances of this class are examined, with their associated bifurcation diagrams illustrated. These findings are supported by numerical simulations. The results suggest that self-exciting systems belong to a broader category of systems governed by threshold nonlinearities. Ultimately, the bifurcation structures observed in this new class are expected to appear in other threshold nonlinear systems. The authors anticipate that this general class will facilitate the development of novel self-exciting systems and provide a foundation for further research into their dynamical properties. Additionally, the paper explores the potential for designing new sensors based on the bifurcation structures of these systems. This work extends the research presented in [1].

This study introduces a free-breathing, motion-corrected 4D (3D plus respiration) T2-weighted turbo spin-echo (T2-TSE) sequence designed for body imaging. The approach employs a self-gating technique to retrospectively reconstruct 4D datasets. To address the inherent trade-off between scan duration and image quality, the method utilizes a high echo train length (ETL) of 128, which is dynamically adjusted based on the number of free-breathing breath-holds. This strategy allows for the acquisition of a 4D T2-TSE dataset within a single breath-hold, delivering superior temporal resolution and image quality. The resulting images are corrected for respiration motion using a non-rigid registration algorithm. Validation was performed on 10 healthy volunteers and 10 patients with liver metastases. The 4D T2-TSE data demonstrated robustness against free-breathing artifacts, enabling the generation of high-quality in-breath, end-breath, and average images. Furthermore, the temporal resolution was sufficient to capture cardiac motion, and the technique proved effective for both healthy volunteers and patients. These findings indicate that the proposed method is a viable solution for body imaging, particularly for the liver, offering a practical alternative to breath-holding. Additionally, the 4D T2-TSE dataset can be segmented into multiple 3D volumes, providing flexibility for various imaging applications. The technique's versatility was further demonstrated by its application to a healthy volunteer with a known liver hemangioma, where the lesion was successfully visualized across different 4D phases. In conclusion, this method represents a promising approach for body imaging, delivering high-quality 4D T2-weighted images without the need for breath-holding. Future research will explore its utility in characterizing liver hemangiomas and assessing tumor perfusion. Model compression is essential for deploying deep neural networks on resource-constrained devices. Data flow-preserving techniques, which maintain the original data flow structure of the target network, have proven highly effective for compression. However, these methods are typically limited to single-stage distillation and cannot be applied to data flow-preserving multi-stage distillation. This paper introduces InDistill, a knowledge distillation approach that applies data flow-preserving strategies to both input and intermediate features. InDistill employs a two-step process: first, it freezes input features from the large model and performs standard data flow-preserving distillation; second, it utilizes the frozen features as an additional teacher to guide the distillation of intermediate features. Experiments on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet demonstrate that InDistill surpasses state-of-the-art methods in both accuracy and compression efficiency. Furthermore, the approach is versatile, supporting various data flow-preserving techniques such as network pruning and channel sharing. This study examines the influence of non-resident grazing on dry-land vegetation dynamics. We introduce a spatially explicit, two-species plant model featuring a resident herbivore and a plant species that are absent in the second scenario. The research investigates how the introduction of non-resident grazers alters the stable configuration of the resident system. Our findings indicate that non-resident grazers can trigger the emergence of novel stable states, including patterns of spatially heterogeneous plant distribution. Furthermore, these patterns can arise through a Hopf bifurcation, resulting in stable oscillations of plant density. We also identify the specific parameter ranges for both heterogeneous spatial distributions and oscillatory dynamics. Finally, we validate these theoretical predictions using real-world data on dry-land vegetation from the Northern Great Plains. The results demonstrate that non-resident grazers can induce both spatial heterogeneity and temporal fluctuations in plant density. These insights are crucial for managing rangelands, as they suggest that grazing can be utilized to maintain plant diversity and prevent the dominance of a single species. Additionally, the model offers a framework for understanding how grazing impacts the stability of dry-land plant communities. Ultimately, this research underscores the necessity of incorporating grazing dynamics into future studies of dry-land plant systems. We investigate adaptive data analysis, a field addressing challenges that emerge when machine learning models are evaluated on data partially generated by the same training process. A primary difficulty involves overfitting to noise within this adaptive data. We analyze the performance of adaptive learners utilizing randomized data structures, specifically focusing on CountSketch, a technique for estimating frequency moments. Our findings demonstrate that adaptive learners employing CountSketch achieve optimal minimax rates for regression and classification tasks. Furthermore, we establish that no algorithm can surpass these performance levels. To our knowledge, this represents the first instance where the efficacy of a randomized data structure is proven in an adaptive learning context. Additionally, we present a reduction from the Online Arm Bandit problem to adaptive learning, which enables the derivation of regret bounds for adaptive learners. We also introduce a novel online algorithm that matches the performance of the optimal offline approach, thereby resolving a longstanding open problem in that area. Finally, we explore the limitations of adaptive learning by constructing a scenario where even randomized methods are compelled to overfit to noise. We introduce ipie, a Python-based auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) software suite designed for the efficient simulation of interacting quantum systems on both CPUs and GPUs. The implementation utilizes an adaptive time step scheme to enhance sampling efficiency and supports both periodic and open boundary conditions. Furthermore, the code is engineered to handle arbitrary quantum system sizes and dimensions, offering the flexibility to simulate quantum systems with arbitrary connectivity. This paper presents a comprehensive overview of ipie, detailing its implementation, benchmarking results, and applications. We demonstrate that ipie achieves high computational efficiency across diverse quantum systems, including the Fermi-Hubbard model, the Bose-Hubbard model, and the Heisenberg model. Additionally, we illustrate ipie's capability to simulate quantum systems with non-trivial connectivity, such as the Kitaev model on a honeycomb lattice and the Heisenberg model on a hypercube lattice. The source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/iee-group/ipie. We anticipate that ipie will serve as a valuable resource for the quantum Monte Carlo community. We investigate a dynamic framework where income-generating agents, referred to as workers, are distributed across a two-dimensional grid. These workers move randomly and earn income based on their location, which is determined by an external field. They trade a portion of their earnings with brokers at a rate $\alpha$, while brokers, driven by an internal field, transition between states at a rate $\beta$. Our analysis examines the system's steady-state behavior, revealing that income distribution is highly sensitive to the $\alpha$ and $\beta$ values. Furthermore, we explore the impact of introducing noise into the external fields governing worker income. Finally, we present numerical simulations of a specific scenario where income follows a Gaussian distribution, observing that the system's behavior aligns with our theoretical predictions. This study is motivated by applications in the Internet of Things, where brokers represent base stations and workers represent mobile devices. Additionally, the framework is relevant to biological systems, such as bacteria consuming nutrients in a grid-like environment. In this context, the bacteria are the income-generating agents, and the nutrient sources act as brokers that can switch between active and inactive states. Our findings indicate that the model's parameters can be tuned to achieve a Pareto-optimal distribution of income. The active and inactive states of the brokers correspond to active and inactive regions of the nutrient field, respectively. We demonstrate that the model's behavior remains consistent across both the IoT and bacterial applications. This study introduces a context-aware approach to model vocal entrainment in dyadic conversations. The method utilizes a Gaussian Process to estimate a speaker's pitch contour based on the interlocutor's prior utterances and subsequently generates a target pitch contour through devoiceing. This desired output is then produced by adjusting the speaker's fundamental frequency via a proportional-integral-derivative (PID) controller. We developed a novel evaluation metric to assess the entrainment of the proposed system, comparing it against existing metrics and those used in prior research. Experimental results indicate that the system successfully entrained to its conversational partner, and the new evaluation metric proved more effective than previous ones for evaluating system entrainment. Furthermore, we conducted a subjective experiment to gather human feedback on the unnaturalness of the generated speech, demonstrating that the system's performance correlated with these human evaluations. Finally, we present a recorded sample of a conversation involving the system to illustrate its performance. These findings suggest that the proposed system and evaluation metric are well-suited for developing natural conversational agents. The code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/keigo-ito1234/voice-entrainment.

We introduce a fully faithful embedding of lambda-S1, the simply-typed calculus of quantum manipulations, into the quantum channel category. This process manipulates the density matrices of pure states as if they were vectors, utilizing the corresponding von Neumann projections. We subsequently examine the categorical model for lambda-S1 and demonstrate that, despite the density matrices of pure states lacking closure under convex combinations, the category of manipulations for these matrices exhibits all the characteristics of a categorical model for a typed lambda calculus. Finally, we outline a method to extend this methodology to more sophisticated programs. (This research was conducted during the first author's visit to the University of Pisa.)

This study examines a Stokes variational inequality arising in glaciology, characterized by a degenerate, semicoercive elliptic operator dependent on a viscosity parameter. The analysis focuses on the convergence of finite element approximations, specifically evaluating the impact of viscosity degradation. The resulting error estimates are nearly optimal, provided the approximation error diminishes sufficiently rapidly. Numerical experiments are conducted to validate these theoretical findings. The work is situated within the framework of glaciology, where a nonisothermal Stokes model for ice flow is employed. This model incorporates a temperature-dependent viscosity that degrades as temperature approaches the melting point, resulting in a semicoercive Stokes system defined on a convex polygonal domain with inhomogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions.
