We introduce Delegated RingCT, a novel ring signature framework designed for privacy-preserving payment systems. This approach substantially lowers the computational and memory demands on participants while maintaining RingCT's capacity to prevent double-spending. Our solution relies on the existence of a trusted setup and utilizes a new ring signature type called "delegated ring signatures." In this model, signers pre-generate a compact set of public parameters and a corresponding proof of knowledge, which are subsequently combined with a signature to form a valid signed ring set. We provide a formal definition and proof of security for these signatures, and we detail the integration of delegated ring signatures with the blockchain to construct a complete Delegated RingCT protocol. Empirical results demonstrate that the per-transaction cost for both the sender and receiver is reduced by a factor of 1000 compared to standard RingCT, with only a minor increase in blockchain storage requirements. Furthermore, we outline a path toward eliminating the need for a trusted setup by proposing a method to generate the required parameters in a trustless environment. This work holds significant potential for enhancing privacy in payment systems and other applications utilizing RingCT. The implementation is available at https://github.com/DelegatedRingCT. We introduce AskewSGD, a novel stochastic gradient descent (SGD) variant designed to train neural networks using low-precision weights. By applying a non-symmetric bias to the low-precision gradient estimator, the method effectively mitigates quantization errors inherent in low-precision training. This approach is particularly beneficial for quantized networks with asymmetric activation functions, such as ReLU, which typically hinder the training stability of standard quantized SGD. Our findings indicate that AskewSGD surpasses existing state-of-the-art techniques for full quantization, including Proximal Low Precision (PLP), BFloat16, and Low Precision with Asymmetric Activation Functions (LPAQ). Furthermore, we demonstrate that AskewSGD can be seamlessly integrated with various quantization and compression schemes, such as quantization-aware training (QAT), to further enhance performance. Empirical results confirm that AskewSGD outperforms these schemes in achieving high accuracy during full quantization training. Additionally, the method proves effective in reducing the memory footprint of pre-trained models, enabling their deployment on resource-constrained devices. Finally, AskewSGD is compatible with dynamic quantization strategies, allowing for the creation of robust quantization-aware models. This paper introduces a novel method to enhance the training of GANs by leveraging the latent space of an autoencoder. We propose a technique that enables a discriminator to access additional information regarding the generated samples. By employing a discriminator with multiple heads, we condition it on the latent representations of encoder autoencoders applied to the generator's outputs. We introduce a straightforward approach to contrast various samplers designed for layering. This comparison relies on the concept of layering, which enables the evaluation of multiple samplers using a single reference sampler. By leveraging this reference, we can compare other samplers without incurring additional computational costs. Furthermore, the layering framework facilitates the comparison of samplers that may not otherwise be directly comparable. Our primary contribution is the introduction of two distinct methods for contrasting samplers within this framework. The first method utilizes the layering of two samplers to define their contrast, while the second employs two nested samplers to achieve the same. We demonstrate that the variance of the layering estimator is proportional to this contrast, thereby providing a clear interpretation of the metric. Additionally, we provide an interpretation of the contrast in terms of acceptance probabilities and establish its relationship with other contrast measures found in existing literature. Finally, we apply these new contrast measures to compare several samplers for non-convex and multi-modal distributions. Distance labeling (also known as distance array) represents a compact and local representation of the distance matrix for a graph. Introduced by Thorup in 2004, it maps every vertex $v$ of a graph $G$ to a label $\ell(v)$ such that the distance between any two vertices $u$ and $v$ can be determined directly from $\ell(u)$ and $\l(v)$ without referencing the graph's structure. While Thorup's original method employed a labeling scheme of size $O(n)$ for an unweighted graph with $n$ vertices, subsequent research has focused on reducing this size to $o(n)$. However, existing schemes are highly sensitive to label corruption; even a single corrupted bit can compromise the entire distance matrix. This paper presents a resilient distance labeling scheme for $n$-vertex undirected graphs with bounded treewidth $w$ that tolerates $k$ corrupted labels. The scheme achieves a space complexity of $O(w^2 n (\log n + k) \log w)$, ensuring that distances remain accurate even when up to $k$ labels are corrupted. This approach is particularly effective for planar graphs, where the treewidth is linear in $n$. Furthermore, the scheme is fully dynamic, allowing for the insertion and deletion of vertices and edges. In the dynamic setting, the algorithm operates in $O(w (\log n + k) \log w)$ time per operation. Additionally, we demonstrate that our scheme is nearly optimal by proving a lower bound of $\Omega(n (\log n + k))$ for the space complexity of any dynamic distance labeling scheme for planar graphs. To our knowledge, this constitutes the first dynamic distance labeling scheme capable of handling label corruptions. Finally, we extend our method to weighted graphs, achieving a space complexity of $O(w^2 n (\log n + k) \log w \log (\Delta + 1))$, where $\Delta$ denotes the maximum edge weight. This scheme is also fully dynamic, with an operation time complexity of $O(w (\log n + k) \log w \log (\Delta + 1))$. We establish a matching lower bound of $\Omega(n (\log n + k) \log (\Delta + 1))$ for the space complexity of any dynamic distance labeling scheme for weighted graphs. This work investigates two-particle correlations within a frequency-domain framework for a driven-dissipative Bose-Hubbard model. The study examines how two-particle density and current evolve over time, analyzing their frequency-domain characteristics and the associated spectral functions. Furthermore, the effects of driving and dissipation on these two-particle observables are explored. The findings indicate that driving and dissipation significantly influence two-particle correlations, with frequency-domain functions exhibiting notable sensitivity to these factors. These results offer valuable insights into the dynamics of two-particle correlations in driven-dissipative quantum systems. Additionally, the methodology employed can be extended to investigate other quantum systems. This paper examines the solvability of second-order elliptic equations in divergence form featuring drift terms. The drifts are represented as sums of an $L^2$ function and a distribution, while the equation's coefficients are defined as functions of a Sobolev space exponent. The analysis focuses on elliptic operators that may lack boundedness. We establish that the dual operator shares the same structural properties and demonstrate that these characteristics remain stable under perturbations by a sufficiently small $L^2$ function. Furthermore, we prove the existence of a unique $W^{1,2}$ solution for the associated divergence equation. As a consequence, we derive $L^p$ estimates for the elliptic equation and establish the solvability of the corresponding Dirichlet problem within a bounded domain. Additionally, we show that the Poisson equation satisfies the necessary conditions. Our findings extend the work of Fabes, J. and R. S. Koch. Additionally, we provide an alternative proof for the solvability of the Dirichlet problem involving elliptic operators with real coefficients, previously established by Fabes and R. S. Koch. Finally, we demonstrate the existence of a positive solution to a specific class of elliptic equations with divergence form. These results are applicable to the study of the Navier-Stokes equations. The methodology employed relies on the theory of Hilbertian spaces and the properties of elliptic operators. The paper concludes with a discussion of the limitations of the current approach and outlines potential directions for future research. Out-of-distribution (OOD) detection is a critical component of machine learning that ensures safety and reliability. While numerous methods have been developed, many rely on the assumption that in-distribution (InD) data follows a Gaussian distribution, an assumption that often fails in practice. This paper introduces a novel OOD detection framework utilizing distributional normal processes (DiNoPro) layers. These layers are trained exclusively on InD data to model its distribution, with the hypothesis that capturing the true data distribution will enhance detection performance. We evaluate our approach on OOD classification tasks using ImageNet and OOD detection tasks on COVERAGE and SHAPES datasets. Our results demonstrate that this framework achieves state-of-the-art performance, particularly on difficult tasks where InD data is limited. The code is accessible at https://github.com/abhishekkumar12345/DiNoPro. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the method's properties and its effectiveness in identifying OOD data. Driven open quantum systems frequently experience heating, which prevents condensation. However, we demonstrate that a specific driving protocol can reverse this trend. By implementing a two-color field on a 1D optical lattice with asymmetric dissipation, we stabilize a Bose-Einstein condensate in the open system. This condensation is driven by a non-equilibrium steady state where the effective temperature is sufficiently low. We further show that this low temperature can be further reduced by selecting a particular initial state, thereby enabling the Bose condensation of an initial pure state. This phenomenon is validated through numerical simulations of a non-interacting Bose-Hubbard model. Additionally, we provide an analytical framework to describe the resulting non-equilibrium steady state. These findings indicate that Bose condensation can occur in non-equilibrium open systems, a result that may have significant implications for quantum information processing. Furthermore, our proposal offers a pathway to generate complex, non-trivial quantum states, such as cat states, within open systems. This capability could facilitate the study of decoherence dynamics in these systems and advance the development of quantum technologies. Finally, we outline a feasible experimental approach to realize this proposal using rubidium atoms. Our work establishes a foundation for investigating non-equilibrium Bose condensation and the associated dynamics. The proposed scheme is also applicable to other platforms, including trapped ions and superconducting circuits. This study establishes a novel Alexandrov-type maximum principle for the complex Monge–Ampère equation subject to a non-negative right-hand side, formulated within a weak setting. This finding yields a unified proof of uniform Hölder continuity for both the Pucci–Sirkani and Cheng–Yau solutions. Furthermore, the methodology is applicable to the complex Monge–Ampère equation with a general right-hand side, thereby providing a comprehensive proof of the uniform Hölder continuity of both solution types in that context as well. Additionally, the enhanced maximum principle facilitates the investigation of the regularity of Alexandrov solutions to the complex Monge–Ampère equation when the right-hand side adheres to a Dini condition. The proof strategy relies on a newly developed technique for handling the approximation of Alexandrov solutions via regularized solutions, alongside a specific approach for managing the error arising from the nonlinearity of the equation. This advancement refines and extends the previously published work of the first author. Finally, the paper presents several applications demonstrating the utility of the primary result. The methodologies employed are also pertinent to the real Monge–Ampère equation. The findings were presented at the International Congress of Mathematicians in Beijing, 2022. This study introduces a statistical framework to examine and contrast the time-domain characteristics of non-repetitive optical clocks. The approach relies on stochastic models for clock noise, which are characterized using statistical metrics such as the allan variance, the time-dependent error distribution, and the error distribution's time evolution. These methods are applied to analyze two specific clock noise models: the $1/f$-walk random walk (WRRW) and the time-dependent white phase random walk (TPRW). The analysis reveals that the TPRW model exhibits a significantly narrower error distribution compared to the WRRW model. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that the TPRW model's parameters can be estimated with high precision by analyzing the time evolution of the allan variance. Finally, the implications of this work for future experimental investigations into optical clocks are discussed. This research is anticipated to provide a valuable foundation for the continued development of optical clocks. Additionally, the code employed in this study is publicly accessible. This study addresses Service Function Chains (SFCs) within Software Defined Networks (SDN) by simultaneously optimizing failure restoration, fault mitigation, and energy-efficient resource management. The proposed framework leverages fog computing to execute real-time restoration strategies, utilizing a centralized controller to dynamically reconfigure network resources. This reconfiguration aims to restore failed services, mitigate faults, and enhance energy efficiency. To achieve this, the authors introduce a novel algorithm that employs a Lagrangian dual decomposition approach to solve the associated optimization problem. The algorithm's performance is evaluated against two baseline methods: a fixed dual decomposition algorithm and a dynamic programming-based approach. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed algorithm outperforms both baselines in terms of failure restoration, fault mitigation, and energy efficiency. Furthermore, the study investigates the impact of fault rates and failure rates on these outcomes. Finally, the paper concludes by outlining potential future research directions. Although loss functions are essential to deep learning, their specific impacts on model performance remain poorly understood. This study investigates how different loss functions affect various components of Markov decision processes (MDPs) by applying them to simple linear models within these environments. We demonstrate that the choice of loss function significantly alters the optimal gradient norm, the optimal learning rate, and the optimal policy. Furthermore, we introduce a straightforward yet effective algorithm designed to automatically identify the most suitable loss function for a given task. Finally, we extend this research to Markov games, revealing that similar findings hold true in this broader context. Our results are supported by both theoretical analysis and experimental validation. The code for this work can be found at https://github.com/ChenYi2000/loss_function_mdp. Holographic error correction codes are a rapidly expanding category of quantum codes, where the most extensively researched class is the holographic tensor network (HTN). These codes are defined by their tensor network architecture, which maintains a constant number of physical qubits per logical qubit and features a bulk subspace characterized by area-law entanglement entropy. However, the bulk of these codes typically exhibits power-law correlations, a trait that has been difficult to approximate. This study introduces hyper-invariant MERA (HiMERA), a novel class of approximate HTNs designed to facilitate the construction of holographic error correction codes with power-law correlations. We demonstrate that the ground state of a spin chain governed by a scale-invariant Hamiltonian can be efficiently represented by HiMERA. Furthermore, we establish that the code subspace of HiMERA possesses a large code distance, thereby functioning as a holographic error correction code. Finally, we examine the physical implications of these findings. Our research indicates that the ground state of a critical spin chain can be effectively modeled by a quantum code, offering a new perspective for investigating critical phenomena. Additionally, this work provides a new framework for developing quantum error correction codes, potentially advancing the design of topological codes. This study investigates the spatial distribution of the Galactic Core Filaments (GCFs) by analyzing the distance between them. The analysis utilizes a catalog of 100 GCFs, selected from a larger sample of 200 to ensure sufficient numbers for statistical reliability. Distances are measured between the closest points of any two filaments, excluding pairs where the distance falls below the minimum of their respective widths. The resulting distance distribution is modeled using a log-normal function, which provides an optimal fit. The distribution's mean is determined to be 1.02 parsecs, with a standard deviation of 0.31 parsecs. These findings suggest that the average separation between GCFs is comparable to the typical size of the central molecular zone (CMZ). Furthermore, the observed spatial distribution is consistent with a scenario where filaments form through the fragmentation of a single, continuous structure. This result supports the hypothesis that the CMZ is a highly turbulent region, where the interaction of multiple scales drives the formation of the observed filamentary structures. Additionally, the study examines the impact of the initial filament catalog on the final statistical outcomes, concluding that the selection of filaments does not significantly influence the results. This indicates that the chosen catalog is representative of the overall population of Galactic Core Filaments. This study addresses the challenge of minimizing transmission system operating costs through optimal voltage reduction, a task complicated by the need to account for voltage-dependent losses and network constraints. To address this, we introduce a novel Integrated Primary-Secondary Distribution Network (IPSDN) that unifies transmission and distribution systems. Within this framework, transmission and distribution operators function as distinct entities, each pursuing its own optimal goals. To facilitate distributed optimization without requiring global network data, we propose a new algorithm utilizing distributed optimization techniques. This approach enables transmission operators to determine optimal voltage setpoints at distribution interconnection points while considering primary-secondary coupling effects. Furthermore, we introduce a novel secondary optimization problem that integrates distribution network constraints into the transmission operator's cost function. Finally, we demonstrate the algorithm's effectiveness through a numerical case study. The results indicate that the proposed method achieves performance comparable to centralized approaches while requiring significantly less information exchange. Additionally, the study highlights the substantial cost reductions achievable through optimal voltage reduction. Finally, we demonstrate how the algorithm can be extended to accommodate various transmission objectives, such as loss minimization and congestion management. These findings underscore the versatility of the proposed algorithm in solving transmission preservation voltage reduction problems. This study examines a multi-armed bandit framework where arm-dependent delays occur with non-random probabilities. The objective is to identify the arm with the shortest expected delay, even though the agent can only observe the realized delay for the selected arm. We demonstrate that a $1$-specialist algorithm achieves a regret of $O(\frac{1}{\Delta}\log T)$, where $\Delta$ represents the minimum gap between expected delays. This result improves upon the best previously known regret bound of $O(\frac{1}{\Delta^2}\log T)$ established by Agarwal et al. (2020). Furthermore, we show that a $\beta$-specialist algorithm yields a regret of $O(\frac{1}{\Delta^\beta}\log T)$ for any $\beta \geq 1$. Finally, we establish a lower bound of $\Omega(\frac{1}{\Delta}\log T)$ on the regret for this problem setting. Our findings indicate that the $\beta$-specialist algorithm is particularly effective when the $\Delta$ is small. The proposed algorithms are straightforward to implement and can be readily adapted to other delayed multi-armed bandit scenarios. We also provide a Python implementation of the $\beta$-specialist algorithm, which is available on GitHub. We introduce a new framework for generating human-like text in dialogue, which relies on two key components: a data-driven model for identifying and correcting grammatical errors, and a generative text model that leverages these corrections to create new, grammatically accurate responses. This approach is particularly effective for scenarios where annotated data is scarce, as it can be trained using only unannotated erroneous responses. By integrating this model into the generation process, we ensure that the text produced is both grammatically correct and semantically faithful to the input. Extensive experiments across multiple dialogue tasks demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms strong baselines in both grammatical accuracy and faithfulness. Furthermore, we show that our model can be seamlessly applied to various text generation architectures without requiring any modifications to their original training procedures. This document serves as a review of Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) based on the Lattice approach, with a specific focus on non-zero temperature and chemical potential. It begins by outlining the theoretical foundations of the QCD Lagrangian within the lattice framework. Subsequently, it examines the primary challenges associated with QCD simulations, including the sign problem, the necessity of reweighting, and the application of improved actions. The discussion then shifts to results derived from these lattice calculations, covering the chiral phase diagram, the behavior of the equation of state, and the phase structure of QCD at finite temperature and density. Finally, the document concludes with an outlook on future research directions. This text is intended to provide a pedagogical introduction to the subject for graduate students and early-career researchers. Where appropriate, references to recent review articles are included to offer further insight. Additionally, an appendix is provided to briefly address the relationship between QCD and the chiral condensate. Throughout the review, the notation and conventions align with those established in the initial sections. This study introduces a novel statistical surrogate modeling approach utilizing chained Gaussian processes to analyze stochastic offshore wind-turbine loads. The model decomposes the complex turbine system into a series of interconnected subsystems, where the output of each stage serves as the input for the next. To address the non-stationary nature of the data generated by each component, the framework employs Gaussian processes conditioned on the previous stage's output. This chained architecture effectively captures the sequential dependencies inherent in the system. The methodology is validated using a high-fidelity numerical simulation of an offshore wind turbine subjected to stochastic wind and wave excitations. Results demonstrate that the proposed model achieves high accuracy in predicting subsystem responses and significantly reduces computational time compared to the original simulation. Furthermore, the framework supports the calculation of statistical moments and probability density functions for turbine outputs, offering valuable insights for reliability assessments. The paper concludes with a discussion of the method's potential for extension to other engineering applications. This study investigates the Izmir earthquake that struck Turkey on October 30, 2010, by analyzing Twitter data. We gathered 1,000 tweets from that day and categorized them into three groups: Earthquake Information, Earthquake Rumors, and Other. Our analysis reveals that the majority of the collected tweets were not related to the earthquake. Furthermore, we observed that users tend to post tweets in bursts rather than at regular intervals. Finally, we demonstrated that the distribution of these tweets over time follows a power law. These findings can assist in developing more effective early warning systems for future natural disasters. This paper introduces a novel channel estimation framework designed for Orthogonal Frequency Division Multiplexing (OFDM) systems operating under conditions of insufficient cyclic prefix and imperfect hardware. Furthermore, the proposed scheme exhibits robustness against the imperfections found in practical RIS hardware. Additionally, the iELM model is lightweight, enabling rapid training and low computational complexity. Finally, the scheme is versatile, supporting various RIS configurations, including uniform and non-uniform amplitude and phase distributions. The integral fluctuation theorem (IFt) for single-energy systems is derived without relying on stochastic thermodynamic assumptions, thereby establishing a specific form of the generalized energy conservation law within nonequilibrium thermodynamics. This approach enables the calculation of entropy production through experimental measurements of heat and work, effectively serving as an "energy accounting" method. Furthermore, an "energy budget" can be determined by measuring only one of these quantities. Additionally, a fluctuation theorem is proven that links the average dissipated energy to the variance of energy exchange, allowing for energy dissipation measurements that do not require tracking individual trajectories. This is achieved by analyzing the energy exchange variance, which yields the same information regarding dissipated energy as the second moment of stochastic thermodynamic variables. Consequently, these findings offer a novel pathway for advancing experimental nonequilibrium thermodynamics. The methodology is demonstrated using a quantum dot charge pump, where energy budget data is derived from measurements of either heat or work. Finally, the results are compared against those of a classical RC circuit. These findings are anticipated to be applicable to both classical and quantum nonequilibrium thermodynamics. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 introduces the IFt; Section 3 derives a fluctuation theorem from the IFt; Section 4 discusses the implications of these results for experimental nonequilibrium thermodynamics; and Section 5 presents the application to a quantum dot charge pump. Quantum machine learning represents a rapidly evolving field that holds the promise of surpassing classical methods in specific computational tasks. This study examines a neural network architecture where quantum data is encoded via pure state preparation within a Hilbert space of dimension $d$. We demonstrate that a quantum perceptron utilizing this encoding can achieve any target error rate $p_e$ with a resource requirement of $k \log_2(d+1)$ qubits, where $k$ denotes the dimension of the input feature space. Furthermore, we establish that for any $d \geq 2$, there exist $k$ linearly independent input vectors that are perfectly classified by the quantum perceptron, yielding an input success rate of $p_{in} = 1$. Leveraging these findings, we prove that the quantum capacity of the quantum perceptron, defined as $C_Q = p_{in} - p_e$, can be maximized at $C_Q = 1$ by selecting an appropriate quantum encoding for the input data. Additionally, we derive an upper limit for the classical capacity of the quantum perceptron, showing that the classical capacity of a quantum system with $k \log_2(d+1)$ qubits is bounded above by $k(d+1)$ bits. Finally, we illustrate that the quantum advantage of this architecture can be realized using a minimal resource configuration of $k=1$ qubit. These results indicate that the quantum advantage of the proposed architecture can be amplified by increasing the number of qubits employed. Our findings are validated through numerical simulations. We introduce a C code generator for ACL2, which is a logic programming language featuring strong interactive theorem proving capabilities. This tool is designed to facilitate the development of verified software by translating ACL2 specifications into executable C code. Our approach utilizes a shallow embedding of C within ACL2, ensuring that C programs are represented as ACL2 theorems. Consequently, the generator leverages ACL2's proof generator to produce C code accompanied by formal proofs of correctness. We demonstrate the tool's effectiveness through a case study involving the development of verified software for a smart home system. The resulting code includes verified C implementations for an I2C driver, an LED driver, and a smart home system model, all accompanied by formal proofs of correctness. A key advantage of this method is that it eliminates the need for separate formalization efforts for both the programming language and its library functions, as the C language is deeply embedded within ACL2. The tool is implemented as a library in ACL2, allowing for the formal verification of its own correctness. The complete implementation, along with all examples and proofs, is accessible via the accompanying repository. The formalization process was conducted using the Coq proof assistant. Our work demonstrates that C programs can be effectively developed using ACL2, and that C code can be formally verified using Coq. This is achieved through a deep embedding of C within Coq, which provides greater modularity and flexibility compared to a shallow embedding. The entire implementation, including examples and proofs, is available in the provided repository. The formalization was performed using ACL2 and Coq, two of the most prominent theorem provers in the field. We conclude that our approach offers a comprehensive solution for the development of verified software, combining the strengths of both proof assistants. The paper concludes by discussing potential future research directions and applications. Specifically, we aim to extend the current implementation to support more complex C programs and to explore the use of automated theorem provers to verify the correctness of the generated code. Additionally, we plan to investigate the application of our method to other programming languages and to examine the potential for using formal methods in the software industry. Finally, we intend to explore the use of formal methods for the development of safety-critical systems, such as those used in aviation and medical devices. The formalization was carried out using ACL2 and Coq, two of the most widely used theorem provers in the field. We believe that our method offers a robust solution for the development of verified software, and we hope that it will inspire further research in this area.

Ramanujan demonstrated that the odd zeta values $\zeta(2k+1)$ for $k=1,2,3,\ldots$ can be expressed using the digamma function evaluated at rational points $\frac{p}{q}$. This note presents a generalization of Ramanujan's findings by expressing these values through the digamma function with arguments involving the Gauss constant $G(a)=\frac{\zeta(0,a)-\zeta(0,1-a)}{2\pi i}$. Additionally, we establish a new identity for the Riemann Zeta function utilizing the Hurwitz Zeta function. Finally, we provide a novel proof of Ramanujan's original theorem. Although the Signal app is widely used, its registration process requires new users to create and remember a 6-digit personal identification number (PIN). This study investigates how 24 enthusiastic Signal users perceive these PINs and their ability to recall them. Participants were asked to describe their experiences with Signal PINs and then attempt to recall a previously generated one. The findings reveal that users hold diverse views on the purpose of PINs, with many believing they serve no function. Additionally, users struggle to remember their PINs, often resorting to guessing. These results suggest that the app's onboarding flow may be unnecessarily complex for casual users. To address this, we propose a design for a user-friendly PIN manager that integrates directly into Signal's onboarding process. The study also offers recommendations for improving user comprehension of the PIN's role and its memorability. Finally, we explore the relationship between users' perceived understanding of the PIN's purpose and their actual ability to recall it. The paper concludes with a discussion of the limitations of these findings. The source code for the PIN manager is available at https://github.com/SignalApp/pin-manager. This study introduces a new approach for integrating functions of the form $f(x)\max(0, \Phi(x))$, where $\Phi(x)$ represents the normalized cumulative distribution function (CDF) of a probability measure $\phi(x)$ defined on a compact interval. This method is particularly valuable for modeling solar irradiance, as the specific structure of $\Phi(x)$ in that context enables a highly accurate and computationally efficient solution. By leveraging the known roots and weights of Gaussian quadrature associated with the measure $\phi(x)$, we derive a quadrature rule for the normalized density function $\phi(x)$ that yields $\Phi(x)$ values at the quadrature points with exceptional precision. Consequently, the integral of $f(x)\max(0, \Phi(x))$ can be evaluated using a small number of function evaluations, achieving relative errors below $10^{-10}$. The primary innovation of this work is the development of a new quadrature rule for functions of the form $g(x)\Phi(x)$, where $g(x)$ is any function integrable with respect to the measure $\phi(x)$. This new rule utilizes the known roots and weights of Gaussian quadrature for the measure $\phi(x)$ to construct a quadrature for $g(x)\Phi(x)$ that achieves the same high level of accuracy. The paper provides a rigorous theoretical analysis of this approach and demonstrates its effectiveness through applications in solar energy integration. A key application involves modeling the probability density function of the daily total solar irradiance received at a specific geographic location, where the measure $\phi(x)$ is defined by a probability distribution determined by the location's latitude and the day of the year. The proposed solar-weighted quadrature enables the precise evaluation of the normalized CDF $\Phi(x)$ at quadrature points, thereby facilitating highly accurate and efficient numerical integration of functions dependent on solar irradiance. Furthermore, the paper illustrates how this quadrature can be applied to determine the probability density function of daily total solar irradiance, which is essential for solar energy system design and analysis. The study concludes with numerical examples that validate the accuracy and efficiency of the proposed method. These results indicate that the solar-weighted quadrature is a powerful tool for solar energy integration, offering both high precision and computational efficiency. Ultimately, this approach provides a robust framework for modeling and analyzing solar irradiance, with significant implications for solar energy system design and analysis. The curvature of a function is a fundamental property that significantly influences the behavior of optimization algorithms. This paper introduces a new class of algorithms designed to efficiently approximate curvature information for both smooth and non-smooth functions. These methods are derived from the generalized Gauss-Newton matrix, offering second-order convergence for smooth functions and providing descent guarantees for non-smooth ones. Furthermore, the proposed algorithms are non-variational, enabling the use of mini-batches for gradient estimation. We demonstrate that these algorithms achieve the same optimal complexity as first-order methods regarding function and gradient evaluations. Additionally, we present a novel application of these algorithms to the training of ResNet models. Experimental results indicate that our approach outperforms existing second-order methods in terms of complexity while maintaining competitive performance in training ResNets. This study examines how grammatical gender influences word representations in neural language models within gender-marking languages. By employing a gender priming paradigm, we demonstrate that gender-related information is readily accessible in both BERT and GloVe vectors for German, Russian, and Spanish. Furthermore, we reveal that gender-ambiguous words activate gender-biased synonyms, a phenomenon that varies across languages. Finally, we analyze the impact of gender on the semantic representations of nouns, highlighting the challenges of disentangling gender from other linguistic features. These findings offer a comprehensive perspective on the gender dynamics within neural language models, with significant implications for developing gender-sensitive resources. We introduce a zero-shot class-level object pose estimation approach that utilizes a pretrained, pose-agnostic, class-agnostic detector. Unlike traditional pose estimation tasks focused on specific object classes or instances, our method addresses the challenge of estimating poses for class-level instances of objects seen for the first time. By leveraging a pose-agnostic detector, we can directly apply our technique to novel classes without requiring additional training. Specifically, we employ a vision-language model to generate natural language descriptions of an object's class, which are then paired with 3D object models to estimate its pose. We validate the efficacy of our approach on a newly created synthetic dataset, ShapeNet-AD, and further demonstrate its success in a real-world scenario by accurately estimating the pose of a class-agnostic detector's view of a chair in an indoor environment. Accurate short-term traffic forecasting is essential for intelligent transportation systems, yet it remains difficult due to the scarcity of data and the need to handle irregular patterns. This paper introduces a new deep learning framework designed to predict traffic conditions using extensive sparse data. The approach relies on two core components: a feature extraction module that identifies traffic patterns through time-series similarity, and a prediction module that leverages these derived features to generate accurate forecasts. To our knowledge, this is the first study to apply a deep learning model for traffic prediction based on similarity-driven feature extraction. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework significantly outperforms existing methods in both prediction accuracy and computational efficiency. Furthermore, the framework's effectiveness in extracting relevant features from extensive sparse data is validated through ablation studies and analyses of learned representations. The film industry is a massive global enterprise that has experienced significant growth in recent years. Despite this, the factors driving a film's success remain a subject of debate. While some argue that data-driven, algorithmic decisions are essential for profitability, others contend that films thrive due to their creative and artistic nature. This study aims to determine whether a film's attributes can predict its success. To achieve this, we introduce a new, comprehensive dataset containing over 10,000 films, each annotated with more than 100 attributes. Our analysis reveals that pre-release characteristics, such as the presence of an A-list actor, director, or specific genres, are strong indicators of box office performance. Furthermore, we find that films with higher critical scores tend to achieve greater box office success, though this correlation is weaker for animated films. Additionally, we observed that release months with high competition often result in lower box office performance. These findings suggest that incorporating pre-release traits into recommendation systems could significantly improve their effectiveness. This study examines a frequency-regulated synchronous machine to demonstrate that it can also serve as an auxiliary device for voltage regulation. The device's efficacy in enhancing voltage stability is validated through numerical simulations of a 30-bus test system. Results indicate that deploying this simple, frequency-coupled control mechanism across the entire network can substantially diminish long voltage sags triggered by large disturbances, such as short circuits. Furthermore, the paper explores the stability characteristics of this frequency-voltage coupled (FVC) regulation, revealing that while local stability is guaranteed, global stability is not assured. Consequently, the research establishes sufficient conditions for global stability and derives the associated stability region. Finally, the influence of network topology on the size of this stability region is analyzed. These findings are corroborated by simulations on both the 30-bus test system and a larger 118-bus network. Ultimately, the study underscores the potential of this straightforward yet effective FVC control to significantly improve the network's ability to withstand large disturbances. The proposed approach is particularly advantageous for systems where traditional primary, secondary, and tertiary frequency control mechanisms are either absent or insufficient. Additionally, the FVC regulation is shown to be compatible with existing frequency control strategies, offering a promising avenue for future power system frequency control. To facilitate these conclusions, the paper also presents a frequency-dependent model for a frequency-regulated synchronous machine. This model is derived from a nonlinear state-space representation of a synchronous machine, utilizing a linearization technique that yields a frequency-dependent linear model. The validity of this linearization is confirmed through simulations. The resulting model is also applied to analyze the stability of a frequency-voltage coupled (FVC) power system. The analysis demonstrates that the FVC model exhibits a frequency-dependent stability region, a feature that is also observed in the full nonlinear model. These findings are supported by simulations on both the 30-bus and 118-bus test systems. The paper concludes by discussing the implications of these results for future FVC power system analysis. Finally, the study addresses the challenge of determining the stability region for the proposed FVC model, which is characterized by a nonlinear vector field with an unstable equilibrium point. This is achieved through the application of a specific theorem from control theory. The theorem is also utilized to examine the stability regions of other FVC power system models. Cyber-physical systems (CPS) are anticipated to become increasingly prevalent in the coming years, with their interconnections forming networks of networks (NoN). These NoN structures are expected to exhibit complex behaviors, including emergent properties, which can be leveraged to enhance NoN performance. This paper introduces a framework designed to model the complex behavior of NoN and to identify the optimal placement of additional CPS to maximize the system's emergent characteristics. The proposed approach utilizes a multi-agent system to manage the NoN, employing a novel algorithm that combines reinforcement learning with a Markov decision process (MDP) to determine the ideal locations for deploying new CPS. The efficacy of this method is validated through a case study involving a smart grid. Results demonstrate that the proposed algorithm successfully identifies optimal positions for new CPS, thereby improving the NoN's emergent properties. Furthermore, the algorithm exhibits superior performance compared to a baseline approach, achieving a 10% increase in the number of NoN satisfying the Markov property and a 15% rise in those satisfying the ergodic property. Additionally, the algorithm shows robustness against uncertainties within the NoN. Ultimately, this study aims to provide a foundation for future research into intelligent NoN. To achieve this, we have developed an open-source software platform that enables the modeling, simulation, and analysis of NoN, along with the implementation of the proposed algorithm. This platform is made available to the research community to facilitate the advancement of intelligent NoN. The source code can be accessed at https://github.com/SmartGrids/SmartGrids.noN. This study investigates the origin of the ultraviolet (UV) and soft X-ray excess observed in blazar spectra, a phenomenon that remains unexplained by standard synchrotron radiation from relativistic electrons. We propose that this excess arises from inverse Compton scattering of the external radiation field, which is partially polarized. To model this process, we employ a Monte-Carlo code previously introduced in [1]. This approach enables the calculation of the energy distribution and polarization state of Comptonized photons emitted by relativistic electrons with a power-law energy distribution. Our results demonstrate that a partially polarized external field can account for the UV/soft X-ray excess in blazar spectra. Furthermore, we show that the polarization degree of this excess correlates with that of the external field, while its polarization angle is determined by the electron Lorentz factor. This paper introduces a practical compression framework for light field (LF) images that leverages disparity knowledge to enhance efficiency. The approach is divided into two main components: a lossless encoder and a lossy decoder. The encoder accepts raw pixel data as input and produces a compact representation suitable for transmission or storage. Upon receipt, the decoder utilizes this compact form to reconstruct the original LF image, with an optional refinement stage that improves quality by incorporating disparity knowledge. To facilitate the transfer of disparity information, we developed a discrete cosine transform (DCT)-based model. This model is trained using disparity maps derived from multi-view images and disparity-preserving patches generated from the compressed data. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both lossless and lossy scenarios. Specifically, in lossless mode, it achieves superior performance over existing techniques. In terms of lossy performance, our framework delivers higher PSNR levels compared to competing approaches. Furthermore, the decoder exhibits robustness against transmission errors, maintaining high performance even when errors are introduced during the transfer of the compact representation. Finally, the framework is highly efficient, capable of processing an LF image at a rate of 10 frames per second on a standard laptop. Small-area estimation is a critical process for low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), where the scarcity of data necessitates the use of auxiliary information to derive reliable estimates. This study evaluates various estimation techniques using a dataset from the 2011 Census of India, focusing on the relationship between population density and area. We compare model-based approaches, specifically small-area spatial linear mixed models, with design-based methods, including generalized regression estimators and small-area domain estimators. The analysis covers model selection strategies, the impact of spatially correlated random effects, and the treatment of zero counts. Results indicate that spatial linear mixed models yield the most accurate estimates, followed by domain estimators, while generalised regression estimators perform the least effectively. Furthermore, spatial linear mixed models demonstrate superior performance over domain estimators when spatially correlated random effects are incorporated. Finally, incorporating spatially correlated random effects enhances estimation accuracy across all model-based methods. These findings are supported by a simulation study. Ultimately, we recommend that practitioners in LMICs adopt spatial linear mixed models, as they offer a robust framework for generating reliable small-area estimates. This study examines privacy-preserving federated learning (FL) within a differential privacy (DP) framework, where a central server coordinates a training process involving multiple non-trusted clients. The objective is to train a model that minimizes a specific loss function while adhering to a defined DP budget. We introduce a federated gradient descent (FGD) algorithm and establish a convergence guarantee for it. Furthermore, we analyze the impact of the DP budget on the algorithm's performance across various client populations. Our findings indicate that privacy constraints can result in a model that fails to converge, particularly when the DP budget is limited. Additionally, we demonstrate that the interplay between DP and FL is influenced by the distribution of data and model parameters across different client groups. Finally, we explore the concept of fairness in DP-FL, illustrating how privacy-preserving FL can inadvertently exacerbate existing biases. We conclude by proposing a method to mitigate these fairness issues. Experimental results validate our theoretical contributions and offer insights into the trade-offs among privacy, convergence, and fairness. Additionally, we find that the neutrino mass matrix elements $|U_{e3}|$ and $|U_{\mu3}|$ are bounded below by $0.01$ and $0.02$, respectively. Finally, we present a detailed analysis of the parameter space within this framework. This study is part of a broader initiative exploring the interplay between dark energy and leptogenesis across various theoretical models. Our results suggest that the interconnection between these phenomena is possible and that the parameter space of the supergravity model can be constrained through this approach. Consequently, this suggests that the interconnection between dark energy and leptogenesis can be tested in future experiments. This paper introduces a data-driven control framework designed to learn control policies for systems with unknown dynamics, utilizing limited data and side information. The proposed method relies on a cost function that integrates both data-driven and model-based components. The model-based term is derived from a known system model, while the data-driven term is based on a data-driven predictor. The study demonstrates that the gradient of this cost function can be expressed as the sum of two parts: one representing the deviation between the data-driven policy and a model-based predictor, and the other capturing the deviation between the data-driven policy and the data-driven predictor. Furthermore, it is proven that minimizing this cost function ensures the policy deviation from the model-based predictor diminishes as the number of data points increases. Finally, the framework is applied to a unified policy learning approach capable of mastering four distinct locomotion tasks—attaining, swimming, walking, and flying—within a single trial. Simulation results confirm that the proposed framework effectively learns policies for all four locomotion tasks. The code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi2000/Unified-Policy-Learning. We investigate the four-point correlation function $\langle\Phi_{1,1}\Phi_{1,1}\Phi_{1,2}\Phi_{1,2}\rangle$ within the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda conformal field model. By utilizing Ward identities, we express the correlation function $\langle\Phi_{1,1}\Phi_{1,1}\Phi_{1,2}\Phi_{1,2}\rangle$ in a form that explicitly displays its dependence on the conformal blocks. Furthermore, we derive a novel set of differential equations governing the conformal blocks. These findings are expected to be applicable to other conformal field theories. Additionally, we present a new numerical verification of the analytic solution for the conformal blocks. This validation was achieved by employing the differential equation method to compute the conformal blocks and comparing them against the conformal blocks derived from the finite-dimensional representation theory of the quantum affine algebra $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_3)$. The latter were obtained through the quantum affine R-matrix method applied to the quantum affine $R$-matrix. Finally, we discuss the application of our findings to the critical $O(n)$ model. Specifically, we demonstrate that the four-point correlation function $\langle\Phi_{1,1}\Phi_{1,1}\Phi_{1,2}\Phi_{1,2}\rangle$ in the $O(n)$ conformal field model can be expressed as a linear combination of the conformal blocks of the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda conformal field model. This result is achieved by employing the free field realization of the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda conformal field model. Consequently, we establish a link between the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda conformal field model and the $O(n)$ conformal field model. Our findings are also relevant to the quantum affine $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_3)$ model. In this context, we show that the four-point correlation function $\langle\Phi_{1,1}\Phi_{1,1}\Phi_{1,2}\Phi_{1,2}\rangle$ can be represented as a linear combination of the conformal blocks of the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda conformal field model. This is accomplished by utilizing the free field realization of the $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_3)$ Toda conformal field model. We also discuss the implications of these results

Relation Networks (RNs) are a recent deep learning approach designed to model complex interactions between inputs by employing a fixed set of relations. While RNs have proven effective for tasks like image retrieval and similarity learning, they are typically trained using standard triplet loss. This paper introduces a novel Relation Generative Adversarial Network (RGAN) that integrates RNs with Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) to enhance their training process. Specifically, we propose a new triplet loss function that leverages the relationship between real and fake samples to refine the representation learning of RNs. By combining the strengths of both architectures, RGANs learn representations that are more robust to variations in object appearance and pose. Extensive experiments on the Stanford Online Products (SOP) and Pascal VOC datasets demonstrate that our method surpasses state-of-the-art performance. Furthermore, we show that RGANs achieve superior results in image classification and generation compared to other GAN variants. The code is accessible at https://github.com/zhongyuanwang/RGAN. Additional details can be found at https://zhongyuanwang.github.io/RGAN/. The paper is available at https://arxiv.org/abs/1901.00220. We also invite contributions to our new dataset, Pascal VOC GANs, available at https://github.com/zhongyuanwang/PascalVOCGANs. This dataset includes 1,000 images from the original Pascal VOC dataset, divided into 80 classes, with 100 images per class. It features 10 object categories (airplane, bicycle, bird, boat, bottle, chair, dining table, elephant, horse, and person) and 10 background classes (bridge, building, cake, chair, cloud, mountain, river, sea, tree, and umbrella). The dataset is divided into 80 images for training and 20 for testing. We also provide a baseline implementation of a DCGAN, which can be trained and tested using the provided scripts. Contributions are welcome, and please contact us at wangzy1992@pku.edu.cn. The dataset and baseline code are available at https://github.com/zhongyuanwang/PascalVOCGANs. For a complex number $\alpha$ where $0 < |\alpha| < 1$, we investigate the structure of Toeplitz algebras formed by the closed linear span of Toeplitz operators with symbols from $L^\infty$ and the analytic function $z^{n+\alpha}\overline{z}^{m-\alpha}$ acting on the weighted Drury-Arveson-type space $\mathcal{B}_\alpha^2$. Furthermore, we extend these findings to the weighted Bergman space $L_a^2(\mathbb{D}, d\mu_\alpha)$, where $\mu_\alpha$ denotes the weighted area measure defined by $d\mu_\alpha = (1-|z|^2)^\alpha dA(z)$ for $-1 < \alpha < \infty$. We demonstrate that the Toeplitz algebras associated with both spaces are isomorphic. Additionally, we establish that the Toeplitz algebras on the Drury-Arveson space and the standard Bergman space are also isomorphic. Finally, we provide characterizations for the commutant of a Toeplitz operator on the weighted Drury-Arveson space and on the Bergman space. As applications, we derive several novel results regarding the commutant of a Toeplitz operator on the Drury-Arveson space. Notably, our results indicate that the commutant of a Drury-Arveson Toeplitz operator is not necessarily invariant under weighted shift operators. To the best of our knowledge, this represents the first instance of such a phenomenon. Furthermore, we characterize the commutant of a Drury-Arveson Toeplitz operator using analytic Toeplitz operators, which are significantly more straightforward to describe than the Toeplitz operators on the space. We also characterize the commutant of a Drury-Arveson Toeplitz operator via analytic Toeplitz operators defined on the polydisc. In the process, we prove that the commutant of a Bergman Toeplitz operator is not necessarily invariant under weighted shift operators, thereby providing the first example of this behavior for Bergman spaces. Additionally, we characterize a Bergman Toeplitz operator's commutant using analytic Toeplitz operators on the unit ball. Finally, we characterize Drury-Arveson Toeplitz operators utilizing analytic Toeplitz operators on the polydisc. These findings offer a comprehensive understanding of the Toeplitz algebra on the Drury-Arveson space

Current object detection methods rely on a fixed set of predefined classes, making it difficult to identify novel objects that were not part of the original training categories. To address this, we introduce a new task called open lexicon object detection, which requires models to recognize both known and novel objects while automatically generating class labels and bounding boxes for the previously unseen ones. To facilitate this, we propose a pseudo bounding-box annotation scheme that supplies only class labels for novel objects, leaving their locations to be inferred by the model. We have created a dataset comprising 1,000 images with 1,000 instances of 100 objects across 20 predefined and 80 novel classes to train and assess our approach. We also present a straightforward baseline method that surpasses a naive detector trained on pseudo bounding-box data. Our contributions include the open lexicon object detection task, the pseudo bounding-box annotation strategy, the established dataset, and the baseline methodology. We present new observations of the ionized gas surrounding the Rho Oph S1 star, utilizing the Hubble Space Telescope's Wide Field Camera 3 to image [OIII] 5007 and H$\alpha$ emission. These data were analyzed alongside archival Hubble Space Telescope and ground-based [SII] 6717/6731 and H$\alpha$ images, as well as existing 12CO J=1-0 and 13CO J=1-0 maps of the region. Our analysis reveals that the ionized gas is confined to a narrow, roughly 10 arcsec wide layer situated between the PDR and the molecular cloud core. This layer exhibits a complex morphology featuring a prominent loop-like structure and a tail extending toward the cloud core. The loop is oriented nearly perpendicular to the cloud core's surface, while the tail aligns parallel to it. We propose that the loop results from the interaction between the ionized gas and the cloud core, whereas the tail is shaped by the magnetic field within the cloud core. Additionally, we identified a layer of atomic hydrogen gas between the ionized gas and the cloud core, which is likely a PDR. This atomic layer is approximately 10 arcsec thick and displays a morphology similar to the ionized layer, suggesting that the ionized layer is embedded within the PDR. The PDR's surface is characterized by a series of ridges and grooves oriented roughly perpendicular to the cloud core's surface. We suggest that these features arise from the interaction between the PDR and the cloud core, driven by the cloud core's surface density structure. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for the morphology of ionized gas around Rho Oph S1. We conclude that the observed features are consistent with a model where the ionized gas is confined to a layer between the PDR and the cloud core, shaped by the cloud core's surface density structure, magnetic field, and the PDR itself. This model also accounts for the morphology of the ionized gas in the vicinity of Rho Oph S1. The study underscores the importance of considering the interaction between ionized gas and the surrounding environment in shaping the morphology of ionized gas around young stars. The results also highlight the need for further observations to better understand the morphology of ionized gas around young stars. The paper concludes with a discussion of the implications of these findings for the morphology of ionized gas around Rho Oph S1 and young stars

This study evaluates two factor models designed to capture the time-varying nature of mortality rates. The first model, an extension of the Lee-Carter framework, utilizes time-varying factor loadings to represent the accelerating pace of mortality decline. The second model employs time-varying principal components to identify the temporal dynamics of latent factors. Both approaches are applied to U.S. death counts across various age and sex groups, with their predictive performance compared against the original Lee-Carter model. Results indicate that the model with time-varying factor loadings outperforms both the standard Lee-Carter model and the model with time-varying principal components in forecasting mortality. Furthermore, this superior model demonstrates robustness when tested on data from other countries. Finally, the model is utilized to estimate life expectancies for the United States, the United Kingdom, and France. These estimates reveal that life expectancies for both sexes in the U.S. are lower than those in the U.K. and the U.S., and that the gap between male and female life expectancies in the U.S. is wider than in the other two nations. Additionally, the study finds that the rate of life expectancy growth in the U.S. has been slower than in the U.K. and France, and that the rate of increase for females has been faster than for males in all three countries. These findings highlight the potential of factor models with time-varying factor loadings for analyzing and predicting mortality trends. The accompanying code is accessible at https://github.com/abhishekkumar2000/Time-varying-factor-loading.

Neural Architecture Search (NAS) has demonstrated significant potential for automatically discovering high-performing models. However, a primary obstacle remains the substantial computational resources required, particularly when utilizing parallel training to evaluate multiple architectures. To address this, various methods have been developed to reduce the number of training iterations. This study investigates a distinct approach that mitigates the need for extensive parallel training by identifying and eliminating inter-architecture interference. We first analyze the performance of architectures discovered by a specific NAS method, revealing that while some are superior, others are inferior due to interference from other architectures. Subsequently, we propose a novel strategy to alleviate this interference, which involves dynamically adjusting the search space to prioritize architectures less affected by competing designs. Experimental results indicate that our approach identifies high-performing architectures more rapidly than the original method. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this performance improvement is achieved with fewer search iterations and reduced search time. Finally, we validate the efficacy of our method across diverse datasets and model types. The code is accessible at https://github.com/ai4mae/interference-free-NAS.

This note provides a negative answer to a question posed by M. R. Bridson and J. D. Groves in their work "On the boundary of a class of CAT(0) spaces," which remains unpublished. Specifically, for any non-compact, properly elliptic CAT(0) surface with non-positive Euler characteristic, there exists a ray that does not converge to a vertex or an end. Consequently, characterizing the boundary of such spaces requires a more robust method than simply relying on their vertices and ends. Furthermore, this result demonstrates that the class of geodesically complete CAT(0) areas is not closed under taking subspaces. To achieve this, we construct a family of examples that are geometrically hyperbolic and exhibit a boundary homeomorphic to the closed unit disk. These examples are derived from the mapping class group of a genus 2 surface and were previously examined by M. Gromov in his book "Metric Structures for Riemannian and Non-Riemannian Spaces." Additionally, we establish that the mapping class group of a once-punctured torus fails to be coarsely embedded into any proper geodesically complete CAT(0) group. This finding offers a novel, non-topological approach to a result by M. Gromov, which was originally established in his book via a topological argument. Finally, we present a characterization of the boundary for a specific subclass of the surfaces under consideration. This subclass consists of surfaces where the mapping class group action on the associated flat bundle is properly discontinuous, and we demonstrate that these groups can be coarsely embedded into Euclidean space. The characterization of their boundary relies on a topological argument. In the process, we also characterize the fundamental groups of these surfaces. Our investigation into these groups is motivated by a question from M. Gromov, which he addressed in his book using a topological argument. We provide a distinct answer by employing a geometric approach. To our knowledge, this constitutes the first purely geometric proof of Gromov's result. This paper introduces a novel approach to assessing translator dependability, which involves modeling the relationship between machine translation quality and translation editing time using a Bayesian linear regression model. The study utilizes a dataset of English-to-French news articles sourced from the WMT14 shared task, where human evaluators rated dependability on a five-point scale. Results indicate that the proposed method outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques. Additionally, the research demonstrates that the Bayesian model yields more reliable predictions than standard linear regression and offers a mechanism to quantify prediction uncertainty. Finally, the paper explores the uncertainty associated with dependability scores derived from evaluators.

We establish sum rules for energy absorption across open quantum systems, including both closed and open channels. These sum rules are derived from the optical theorem and the conservation of energy within open-channel eigenstates. The findings are applicable to diverse contexts, such as quantum transport, absorption in quantum dots, and energy absorption in quantum Hall edge states. Furthermore, we demonstrate that energy absorption is governed by the imaginary parts of the self-energies of the scattering system. Finally, we illustrate the utility of these sum rules through an example of a quantum dot coupled to two reservoirs. In this scenario, we show that the energy absorption of a quantum dot connected to a superconducting reservoir is constrained by the density of states of that superconducting reservoir. Additionally, we examine the implications of these findings for quantum dots linked to chiral edge states. In this specific case, we observe that the energy absorption of the dot is bounded by the density of states of the chiral edge state, which is contingent upon the dot's coupling to the reservoir. These results indicate that the energy absorption of a quantum dot is intrinsically linked to the properties of the reservoirs to which it is coupled. Consequently, this suggests that the energy absorption of quantum dots can be engineered by adjusting the characteristics of the reservoirs. This insight could prove valuable for the design of quantum devices requiring controlled energy absorption. Overall, our findings provide a comprehensive framework for understanding energy absorption in quantum systems, with potential applications spanning quantum computing, quantum information processing, and quantum sensing. Our results offer a robust theoretical foundation for the development of quantum devices with optimized energy absorption properties. By leveraging the sum rules for energy absorption, researchers can design quantum devices with enhanced efficiency and performance. This study examines the optimal pricing strategy for a lottery ticket within a framework where an investor, potentially influenced by behavioral biases, anticipates the future performance of the ticket. The analysis reveals that when an investor expects a future rise in the jackpot, the optimal ticket price will be lower than the expected value of the lottery. Conversely, if the future jackpot is expected to decrease, the optimal price will exceed the expected value. Furthermore, the model demonstrates that investor behavior is highly sensitive to the probability of future jackpot increases, leading to a scenario where multiple equilibria can exist. Finally, the paper explores the implications of these findings for policymakers. Specifically, it suggests that altering the probability of jackpot winning can significantly influence investor behavior, thereby affecting both the lotto's revenue and its potential for raising funds for public purposes. Additionally, the study indicates that changes in the number of required players for jackpot sharing can substantially impact investor behavior. These results underscore the critical role of policymakers in shaping lottery outcomes. Ultimately, the proposed model offers a valuable tool for assessing the efficacy of various policy interventions. For instance, it can be utilized to evaluate the effects of promoting the lottery as a means of wealth accumulation or as a method for educating the public about the risks of gambling. Moreover, the model can help determine the optimal timing for purchasing tickets. Finally, the framework provides insights into the appropriate level of investment required to achieve specific social objectives, such as generating revenue for the government or funding charitable causes. The model can also be adapted to analyze the impact of advertising campaigns on investor behavior. Finally, the study highlights the need for further research to better understand the complex relationship between investor behavior and lottery policy. This includes investigating the effects of investor demographics, education levels, and income on gambling behavior, as well as the impact of investor sentiment and the broader economic environment. Additionally, the role of investor psychology and the influence of social and cultural factors on lottery participation warrant further investigation. Ultimately, the proposed model serves as a valuable tool for policymakers seeking to maximize the social benefits of lotteries while minimizing potential negative consequences. By utilizing this framework, policymakers can make informed decisions that balance the interests of investors, the government, and society as a whole. Ultimately, the model provides a foundation for developing effective policies that promote responsible gambling and ensure that lotteries serve their intended social functions. By leveraging this framework, policymakers can create strategies that encourage informed decision-making, foster responsible gambling habits, and ensure that lotteries contribute positively to societal goals. However, its application to spherical data is constrained by t-SNE's reliance on Euclidean distance, which is not suitable for this context. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel t-SNE variant called spherical t-SNE (VMF-SNE), which substitutes the Gaussian distribution with a von Mises-Fisher distribution. We evaluated VMF-SNE against t-SNE and other methods using both synthetic and real-world datasets. The experimental results demonstrate that VMF-SNE surpasses t-SNE in preserving the underlying data structure and outperforms competing methods on certain datasets. We examine the two-dimensional Fermi polaron, consisting of a mobile impurity interacting with a Fermi sea of mobile particles via a contact potential. By extending the diagrammatic expansion originally formulated by Solyom and Fazekas for the three-dimensional case, we derive the corresponding series for two dimensions. Utilizing a diagrammatic Monte Carlo approach, we compute the series and determine the energy of the polaron's ground state. Our findings reveal a strong dependence of the polaron energy on the ratio of interaction strengths between the impurity and the sea particles, a feature that contrasts with the three-dimensional scenario. Furthermore, we observe that the series converges rapidly for both attractive and repulsive interactions, although the rate of convergence is not uniform across all parameter values. We also investigate the impact of a magnetic field on the system, demonstrating that the polaron energy exhibits a quadratic dependence on the field at low levels, consistent with Landau diamagnetism. Finally, we analyze the behavior of the series expansion near the point where the polaron energy equals the scattering threshold, identifying a divergence that signals a second-order phase transition. This divergence is characterized by a critical exponent of approximately 0.6, which aligns with the critical exponent of the 2+epsilon expansion. Additionally, we explore the possibility of a quantum critical point within the phase diagram. These results are compared against existing theoretical and numerical studies. Finally, we discuss the potential for extending this methodology to more complex systems, such as Bose-Bose and Fermi-Fermi mixtures. This work is based on the research presented in [1].

Quantum emulation of fermionic systems is essential for investigating complex many-body phenomena. While quantum chemistry applications have been extensively researched, fermionic systems outside this domain remain underexplored. This study introduces a hybrid digital-analog quantum computing approach to emulate such systems on quantum hardware. We demonstrate the successful emulation of a one-dimensional spin-1/2 Heisenberg model featuring strong Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interactions. Furthermore, we examine the relationship between the model's ground state and its phase diagram. Our findings indicate that the critical points of the phase diagram can be identified by measuring the two-point correlation function in the emulation. Additionally, we show that the ground state at these critical points can be prepared using the hybrid digital-analog method. Finally, we explore the potential of this emulation for investigating spin-liquid phases. These results highlight the broad applicability of the hybrid digital-analog quantum computing method for fermionic systems. This paper investigates graph traits, defined as mappings from the set of unlabelled graphs to the set of unlabelled partitions. Furthermore, we establish that such a pure series corresponds to the inverse of the Poincar\'e series of the trait defining it, and we derive an explicit formula for it. Additionally, we prove that the inverse of a Poincar\'e series belongs to the ring with integer coefficients of all series with integer coefficients, and we provide an explicit formula for this inverse. Finally, we present a formula for the inverse of a general trait series as a sum of "binomial" series, where the summation indices are the terms in the unique decomposition of the original series into pure traits. As an application, we offer a new proof of the identity linking the Poincar\'e series of unlabelled partitions to that of unlabelled cyclically symmetric partitions. We demonstrate that the components of this link correspond precisely to the vertices of the associated Veech surface, and we examine the link's crossings in relation to the holonomy trajectories on that surface.
