This paper introduces a new framework for solving inverse problems within nonuniform sparse frameworks, utilizing a proximal mean approach. The proposed method, named Proximal Sparse Mean Network (NuSPAN), is applied to reconstruct seismic reflectivity from incomplete data. By integrating a proximal mean with a proximal gradient, the framework effectively manages nonuniform sparse means. NuSPAN is evaluated against two baseline methods: the proximal mean network (SPAN) and a data-driven approach called seismic reflectivity reconstruction (SRR). Numerical experiments demonstrate that NuSPAN surpasses both SPAN and SRR in accuracy and computational efficiency. Furthermore, the application of NuSPAN to real-world seismic data confirms its superiority over SPAN. These findings indicate that NuSPAN serves as a robust solution for addressing inverse problems in nonuniform sparse frameworks. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi2000/NuSPAN. This paper investigates semigroups of composition operators acting on spaces of analytic functions featuring square-integrable boundary derivatives, with a specific focus on the invariant subspaces BMOA and small-BMOA. This paper aims to develop a theory of non-uniform integrability that extends the standard concept of integrability by maintaining key properties such as monotonicity and completeness, while also introducing novel ones like continuity. Central to this effort is a specific $\sigma$-field termed "non-uniformly integrable measurable sets," which enables the construction of a non-uniform integrator for the non-uniform integral. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the non-uniform integrator functions analogously to the standard integrator within various fundamental theorems of integration. Ultimately, we apply this framework to address significant problems in analysis, including non-uniform variants of the dominated convergence theorem, monotone convergence theorem, Fubini theorem, and Lebesgue's decomposition theorem. Additionally, we investigate non-uniform integration with respect to a non-negative $\sigma$-finite measure and a non-negative monotone function, deriving corresponding non-uniform versions of the Radon-Nikodym theorem and the second fundamental theorem of calculus. Finally, we outline several open questions and potential directions for future research in this emerging field. Notably, the non-uniform integral and non-uniform measure introduced here are distinct from, and more general than, the local integral and local measure concepts found in existing literature.

Formal methods are recognized for their ability to detect design flaws early and ensure system correctness, yet they remain underutilized in software development due to their complexity and the high costs associated with training personnel. This paper introduces CitySpec, a web-based service designed to automatically translate requirements into formal specifications. By leveraging the open-source tools ProB and Kermeta, CitySpec facilitates the rapid adoption of formal methods, enabling non-experts to benefit from this approach. The study presents the architecture of CitySpec, outlines a development roadmap, and demonstrates its functionality through a practical case study. Ultimately, this work aims to inspire further research into tools that make formal methods more accessible and to encourage their integration into the software development lifecycle. CitySpec is available at https://cityspec.net. The corresponding source code and documentation can be found at https://github.com/ETIT-2019/cityspec. Additional details regarding the tool and its development are provided in reference [1].

Current pre-trained vision-language models (VLMs) are typically trained using image-text pairs from large-scale datasets, where the text is a direct description of the image. However, relying solely on these descriptions is insufficient for robust VLMs, as they often fail to capture the full range of information needed for various downstream tasks. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel training strategy called Visual-assisted Text Training (VT-Training). This approach leverages both image-text pairs and visual-assisted text (VA-Texts) to enhance the performance of pre-trained models. Specifically, VA-Texts are generated by combining images with text prompts to provide a more comprehensive context. We demonstrate that incorporating VA-Texts into the training pipeline significantly boosts the capabilities of existing VLMs. Extensive experiments on multiple downstream tasks reveal that our method boosts the performance of pre-trained models by up to 10.5% on image classification and 12.5% on visual question answering. The code is accessible at https://github.com/lyg1999/VT-CLIP. Furthermore, we release a new dataset comprising 10 million visual-assisted text-image pairs, known as VT-Data, to support our methodology. This study examines the impact of operator noise on the convergence of the operator stochastic gradient method within a general noisy matrix framework. Transitioning from the standard stochastic gradient approach in Euclidean space to an operator-based method in a Hilbert space introduces significant challenges, primarily because the absence of a trace inner product prevents the straightforward application of standard convergence analysis techniques. To address this, we introduce a novel analysis framework utilizing the operator norm and a specific operator transition. This method accommodates various forms of operator noise, including those arising from stochastic operators and random matrix ensembles. We demonstrate that this framework effectively recovers established results in the literature while also enabling the derivation of new findings. Furthermore, we explore the application of our framework to the analysis of the operator proximal stochastic gradient method. Our findings indicate that operator noise can either accelerate or impede convergence, contingent upon the specific characteristics of the noise. Finally, we validate our theoretical results through numerical experiments. The primary contributions of this work are threefold: (i) we develop a general framework for analyzing operator methods in noisy matrix settings; (ii) we establish convergence rates for the operator stochastic gradient method in this framework; and (iii) we extend this framework to analyze the operator proximal stochastic gradient method. We introduce a new algorithm designed to identify DNA patterns that are potentially relevant to specific diseases. This method operates by training a deep neural network on one disease while simultaneously training an identical network on multiple others. The system's objective is to learn a shared representation that is highly predictive across all diseases without explicitly searching for or requiring prior knowledge of these patterns. Consequently, the algorithm functions as an unattended system, functioning similarly to the human visual cortex, which processes visual input without a dedicated search mechanism. We demonstrate that this approach successfully identifies DNA patterns known to be relevant to the specific diseases under consideration. Furthermore, we show that these patterns exhibit a high degree of specificity to each individual disease, thereby providing a novel method for developing DNA pattern models that are specific to particular conditions. Finally, we illustrate that the discovered patterns can be utilized to predict the involvement of other diseases in new samples. Our results indicate that the patterns identified by this method are more specific to a given disease than those found by current state-of-the-art techniques. Additionally, we demonstrate that the patterns detected by this method align with those identified by human experts. We anticipate that this method will facilitate the discovery of numerous new DNA patterns, offering a fresh perspective for future research in the field. The surface termination of $V_2O_3$ significantly influences its electronic characteristics. By employing molecular beam epitaxy to grow epitaxial $V_2O_3$ films on Al$_2$O$_3$(0001) substrates, we demonstrate that the metal-insulator transition in these films is contingent upon the specific termination of the underlying $Al_2O_3$ buffer layer. Furthermore, we show that the surface termination of the $V_2O_3$ films themselves can be engineered to exhibit either a $V$-terminated or an $AlO_x$-terminated configuration. X-ray photoemission spectroscopy reveals that the surface electronic structure of these films is dictated by their termination: $V$-terminated films display a half-filled $d$-orbital band at the Fermi level, whereas $AlO_x$-terminated films exhibit a surface state within the band gap. These findings offer new insights into the surface electronic properties of ultrathin transition metal oxides and their potential applications in spintronics. Additionally, they provide a novel approach for controlling the metal-insulator transition in $V_2O_3$ films. This study introduces the Clebsch representation for a broad class of Lie-Poisson systems, which are characterized by the co-adjoint orbits possessing co-dimension equal to the rank of the underlying Lie algebra. The derivation utilizes the co-adjoint orbit method to establish the necessary co-Clebsch variables. Furthermore, the text examines the application of this framework to ideal hydrodynamics and the Euler equations governing rigid body dynamics. A key advantage of the resulting formulation is that it renders the Casimir invariants explicit, thereby clarifying the mechanism by which they contribute to the system's conservation laws. Additionally, the Casimir invariants can be explicitly determined in specific instances, such as the co-adjoint orbits of SO(3). Finally, the work explores the relationship between these co-Clebsch variables and the classical integrability of the systems. Specifically, it demonstrates that for the Euler equations, the co-Clebsch variables can be selected to align with the classical integrals of motion, thus recovering the classical Clebsch variables. This finding offers a novel perspective on the connection between conservation laws and integrability. Finally, the text addresses the challenge of identifying co-Clebsch variables for general Lie-Poisson systems, a task that reduces to solving a system of first-order partial differential equations. The solvability of this system is analyzed, and a specific class of Lie algebras is identified where the equations can be solved explicitly. Finally, the text concludes by outlining potential future research directions. The work is supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China (Grant No. 11971390). This paper introduces a compressible conservation law framework designed for hyperbolic conservation laws incorporating lower-order terms. This method is applied to various problems within viscous fluid dynamics, including the derivation of entropy-satisfying finite volume schemes for compressible barotropic viscous fluids and the development of a new entropy-based scheme for the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations. Furthermore, the framework enables the construction of finite volume schemes that adhere to the maximum principle, a property essential for the isentropic compressible Navier-Stokes equations. The study also examines the relationship between these maximum-principle-based schemes and entropy schemes, demonstrating that the former can be derived as a specific instance of the latter. Additionally, the existence of entropy solutions for the compressible Navier-Stokes equations is reviewed, followed by an analysis of the entropy condition for the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations. Finally, the proposed finite volume schemes are demonstrated to converge to solutions that satisfy the entropy condition. These findings collectively provide a robust approach for the numerical resolution of viscous fluid dynamics equations. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 outlines the conservation law framework; Section 3 addresses entropy conditions for incompressible Navier-Stokes equations; Section 4 details the entropy framework for viscous fluids; and Section 5 presents numerical results. Appendix A provides a concise overview of entropy solutions for the compressible Navier-Stokes equations. We introduce a novel chromatic symmetric polynomial for Dyck paths, grounded in the concept of colored cells. Leveraging the connection between standard Young tableaux and colored cells within straight shape tableaux, we derive a $q$-analogue of Carlitz's $q$-rook numbers. This $q$-analogue not only recovers the count of standard $k$-tuples of non-attacking rooks on a $n \times n$ board but also enumerates $k$-tuples of non-attacking colored rooks. Furthermore, it extends Carlitz's findings regarding the connection between chromatic polynomials and $q$-rook numbers. Finally, we establish the symmetry of our proposed chromatic polynomial for Dyck paths. This result follows from the symmetry of our $q$-analogue, which is demonstrated by calculating the transition matrix between two natural bases for the space of $q$-colorings of $k$-tuples of non-attacking colored rooks. The symmetry of this transition matrix is proven using the $q$-Whitney numbers of the second kind. Additionally, we provide a direct combinatorial proof of the symmetry of chromatic polynomials for $k$-tuples of non-attacking partitions. Our findings are also applicable to the chromatic polynomials of $k$-tuples of non-attacking Dyck paths. This work is partially supported by the National Science Foundation under grant DMS-1901635. This paper introduces the Orientation Convolutive Network (OCN), a new architecture designed to enhance image classification performance. OCN achieves this by integrating two specialized convolutional layers: the Orientation Convolutive Layer (OCL) and the Rotation Convolutive Layer (RCL). The OCL is engineered to extract features that are invariant to image translation, while the RCL is responsible for identifying orientation cues. We demonstrate that these layers can be seamlessly embedded within existing convolutional networks, such as LeNet, without altering their original parameters. Furthermore, we validate the efficacy of this approach through experimental results on the MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets. Our findings indicate that the OCN model attains a test accuracy of 99.7% on MNIST and 91.5% on CIFAR-10, surpassing the performance of standard LeNet. Additionally, we show that OCN maintains robustness against both translation and rotation transformations. Finally, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the filters learned by the OCL and RCL, revealing that they successfully capture distinct and complementary features. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/abdelrahman-ahmed/OCN.

The rapid global spread of the novel coronavirus (COVID-19) has caused significant loss of life and economic damage. While CT imaging is a standard method for diagnosing pneumonia, it is not specific to COVID-19. To address this, we introduce a deep learning framework that leverages human-level diagnostic capabilities to automatically identify the disease from CT scans. Our approach utilizes a Two-stage Time-distributed Capsule Network (TDCN) to extract and aggregate hierarchical features, ensuring that sub-features are hierarchically aligned with high-level ones. This architecture is trained using a novel ensemble dataset of 1,000 annotated CT images. Evaluated on a test set of 100 CT images, our model achieves an accuracy of 96.00%, outperforming other state-of-the-art methods. This study examines the spatial efficiency of Low-Earth Orbit (LEO) satellites, which are essential for delivering broadband connectivity to remote areas. We introduce a method for calculating the number of satellites required to cover a specific region, utilizing a geometric model that incorporates the satellites' communication range and orbital altitude. Our findings indicate that for a given location, increasing the count of satellites in a single orbit does not significantly enhance space utilization. Instead, achieving better spatial efficiency is more effectively accomplished by deploying fewer satellites across multiple orbits. This approach offers a more economical solution for delivering broadband services to remote communities. The proposed methodology is applicable to any region on Earth. As a practical demonstration, we applied this technique to determine the optimal number of satellites needed to serve the island of Madagascar. Furthermore, we have developed an open-source Python package to facilitate these calculations. The package includes a function that accepts geographic coordinates and calculates the minimum number of satellites required to cover that area. We have also included a case study for Madagascar within the package's documentation. This work was conducted as part of the 2021 Google Summer of Code program. This paper derives formulas for the expected value and variance of the sample correlation coefficient across all possible data arrangements. By leveraging symmetry properties of the multivariate normal distribution, we establish these formulas for any dimension $p \geq 2$ and sample size $n \geq 2$. Additionally, we propose an efficient algorithm to compute these results for arbitrary values of $p$ and $n$. The study includes numerical examples to demonstrate the derived formulas and examines the cases where the expected value equals zero and the variance is maximized. Finally, we generalize our findings to scenarios involving the k-th moment for $k \geq 2$. This approach yields a polynomial equation of degree $n$ with rational coefficients, from which the k-th moment can be calculated using only basic arithmetic operations. We also provide an example for $p=3$ and $n=5$ to illustrate this methodology. Furthermore, we derive formulas for the k-th cross-moment, defined as $E[\prod_{i=1}^{k} \rho_i]$, where $\rho_i$ represents the sample correlation between the $i$-th and $(i+1)$-th vectors. These results are expressed through the determinants of matrices containing the expected values of the products of the corresponding elements of the respective vectors. Finally, we extend these findings to samples drawn from a general multivariate distribution. In this context, we derive expressions for the k-th cross-moment in terms of the k-th central mixed-moment, which is defined as the expected value of the product of the deviations of the corresponding elements from their respective means. We also examine the conditions under which the k-th cross-moment vanishes. To our knowledge, these findings represent novel contributions to the field. Additionally, we present a conjecture regarding the conditions required for the k-th cross-moment to achieve its maximum value. Our results indicate that for $k=2$, the expected value of the sample correlation is zero, and the variance is maximized when the sample correlation coefficients take on the values $\pm 1$. We also explore the implications of these findings for the k-sample problem. Finally, we provide R code to compute the k-th moment and k-th cross-moment for any given $k$, along with a conjecture concerning the conditions under which the k-th cross-moment is zero. We introduce an extension of the $S$-matrix approach to general relativity that incorporates massive higher-spin particles. This framework maintains the core principles of general relativity—specifically, the invariance of physical laws under arbitrary coordinate transformations and the equivalence of all reference frames—while offering a more explicit formulation of these concepts. Furthermore, we propose an $S$-matrix theory that surpasses general relativity by including a finite number of massive higher-spin particles. This theory adheres to the same fundamental tenets as general relativity, thereby providing a potential foundation for quantum gravity. Additionally, we explore a broader class of theories that generalize these fundamental tenets, which could serve as the theoretical basis for physics beyond the standard model. Finally, we outline the fundamental challenges that must be addressed to develop an $S$-matrix theory of quantum gravity and beyond. This article serves as a pedagogical introduction to our recent research on $S$-matrix theories involving massive higher-spin particles. It does not claim to offer a comprehensive overview of the field, but rather aims to highlight the fundamental issues and potential solutions relevant to the construction of an $S$-matrix theory for quantum gravity. We conclude by discussing the open questions and possible future directions within this area. Throughout the paper, we provide references to the original literature. While the discussion is primarily conceptual, we also include some technical details. We begin with an introduction to the $S$-matrix approach in quantum field theory, followed by an overview of its application to general relativity. We then examine the problem of constructing an $S$-matrix theory for quantum gravity, followed by a discussion of extensions beyond this framework. Finally, we address the challenges associated with building an $S$-matrix theory for quantum gravity and beyond. This study addresses the uniform stabilization of $n$-dimensional Navier-Stokes equations, subject to finite-dimensional feedback controls within a bounded region $\omega \subset \Omega$. The domain $\Omega$ is defined as a bounded open subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ with a $C^{1,1}$ boundary. The equations are formulated within critical $L^q$-based Sobolev and Besov spaces, where $q$ satisfies the condition $2\leq q\leq \frac{2n}{n-2}$ for dimensions $n\geq 3$, or $n=2$. The analysis demonstrates that the Navier-Stokes equations can be uniformly stabilized around the zero solution by employing a linear feedback control strategy confined to an interior, finite-dimensional subspace. This approach utilizes an explicit formula for the feedback control, which relies on the Riesz representation operator and a specific eigenbasis of the Stokes operator. The dimension of this control subspace is determined by a threshold value derived from the desired stabilization rate and the system's parameters. Furthermore, the required size of this control subspace is shown to be independent of the initial data. These findings extend and complement previous research by the authors, which focused on stabilization within $L^2$-based Hilbert spaces. The current work utilizes the same stabilization methodology but applies it within broader functional settings. The results are applicable to both the Navier-Stokes equations and the linearized Navier-Stokes equations. The paper begins by introducing the necessary notation and defining the functional spaces used throughout the analysis. Subsequently, the authors establish the well-posedness of the Navier-Stokes equations within these spaces and derive essential estimates. Finally, the uniform stabilization results are presented, accompanied by an explicit formula for the feedback control law. The paper concludes with an analysis of the dimension of the control subspace and its relationship to the desired stabilization rate. Additionally, an appendix provides an alternative proof of the uniform stabilization result using a different approach. This alternative method offers a more direct derivation of the stabilization rate and control subspace dimension compared to the primary approach. The authors believe this alternative proof provides valuable insights for future research in the field. The paper also includes a discussion of the limitations of the current approach and potential directions for future work. Finally, the authors acknowledge the contributions of several colleagues who provided valuable feedback and suggestions during the preparation of this manuscript. Their input has been instrumental in improving the quality and clarity of the results presented in this work.

InAs quantum wells (QWs) situated near the surface are extensively utilized for terahertz emission and detection. However, the Fermi level in these near-surface structures is typically pinned near the conduction band edge due to the high density of two-dimensional electron gas (2DEG) states. This study demonstrates that the Fermi level can be pinned near the valence band edge in a near-surface QW by employing a wide bandgap barrier. This approach is achieved through the use of a GaAsAlAsAlAs superlattice barrier, which possesses a bandgap exceeding that of InAs. The resulting configuration enables the creation of a surface barrier with a height surpassing the terahertz photon energy, thereby facilitating the efficient extraction of carriers from the QW. This capability is crucial for enhancing the performance of terahertz quantum well devices. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the spin lifetime of carriers in these near-surface QWs remains comparable to that of bulk materials. This finding is significant for developing spintronic devices utilizing near-surface InAs QWs. The results were obtained using magneto-optical Kerr effect (MOKE) spectroscopy. Our findings indicate that the MOKE signal originates from the quantum well rather than the barrier, as evidenced by the observation of a two-peak signal at low magnetic fields, which corresponds to the Landau levels of the QW. Additionally, the signal exhibits a strong dependence on the incident light polarization, a characteristic typical of magneto-optical Kerr signals. Finally, the signal displays a pronounced sensitivity to the thickness of the barrier, a feature also consistent with quantum well behavior. These results collectively confirm that the signal arises from the quantum well. The observed spin lifetime is approximately 10 ns, a value similar to that of bulk InAs. This is attributed to the narrow bandgap of InAs, which results in a low spin-orbit coupling constant. Conversely, the barrier's wide bandgap leads to a high effective mass and a high spin-orbit coupling constant, resulting in a significantly shorter spin lifetime of less than 1 ns. These findings are consistent with theoretical predictions. The Quick Sinkhorn (QST) algorithm serves as a practical and efficient method for approximating solutions to the Optimal Transport (OT) problem. However, it yields inaccurate results when applied to fully-rank triangular matrices, a scenario that arises frequently in applications. This paper demonstrates that QST fails to precisely solve the OT problem involving collinear measures, a condition inherent to fully-rank triangular matrices. We introduce the Collinear Quick Sinkhorn (CQST) algorithm, which is proven to converge to the precise solution. Furthermore, we establish that CQST operates in linear time, $O(n)$, and utilizes constant memory, $O(1)$. These findings are complemented by an explicit formula for the OT map corresponding to collinear measures. Additionally, we present a new algorithm that precisely solves the OT problem for two Gaussian distributions in $O(n)$ time while consuming $O(1)$ memory. Finally, we validate our theoretical results through numerical experiments. To our knowledge, this work represents the first precise linear-time algorithm for solving the OT problem between two Gaussian distributions. The AU Microscopii (AU Mic) system serves as a critical benchmark for understanding the evolution of planetary systems around active stars. This study presents Far Ultraviolet (FUV) observations of AU Mic obtained with the Cosmic Origins Spectrograph (COS) on the Hubble Space Telescope, covering a 12-year span that includes two distinct eruptive events. We analyzed the FUV spectrum to determine the star's temperature, density, and ionization state, while also examining the variability of the FUV flux and its correlation with optical and near-infrared (NIR) data. Our results indicate that the FUV flux is primarily driven by the chromosphere, which is heated by magnetic reconnection. The spectral characteristics reveal a hot, dense, and neutral chromosphere, with the FUV emission peaking at a temperature of approximately 10,000 K. During eruptions, the FUV flux increases by a factor of 100 to 1,000, driven by a surge in the hot, dense neutral chromospheric component. We observed a strong correlation between the FUV flux and both H-alpha and H-band emissions, suggesting that the chromosphere is the source of the hot gas responsible for NIR excess. Furthermore, we detected a significant correlation between the FUV flux and the H-alpha equivalent width, implying that the hot gas is optically thick. Finally, we compared our findings with the orbital positions of AU Mic b and c to assess the potential impact of the star's chromospheric activity on these planets. Our analysis suggests that AU Mic b and c reside in a region where the chromospheric gas is likely optically thin, resulting in a lower mass-loss rate than previously estimated. Consequently, the chromosphere may have played a more significant role in the early evolution of the system than the corona. These results underscore the necessity of incorporating chromospheric activity into models of planet formation and evolution. The data presented here are accessible via the MAST archive. This paper investigates the dynamics of a charged particle moving through a non-magnetized, highly conductive substance medium. In this environment, the particle's electric field is suppressed by the medium's conductivity, causing it to lose energy via a novel mechanism termed "response drag." The radiation emitted during this process is characterized by "response" and "screening" features. The derived response drag force exhibits a non-relativistic limit that resembles air friction drag, while the total radiated energy scales with the square of the charge. Furthermore, this new drag mechanism competes with both frictional and ionization drag; however, it dominates over ionization drag across all velocity regimes. Additionally, the radiation's angular distribution displays a distinctive pattern known as "screening." Finally, the paper explores the potential for using this new radiation type as a diagnostic tool for substance media. A corresponding computer program, written in Python, is also provided. These findings may have significant implications for particle transport in highly conductive media, such as the dense plasma jets utilized in laser-plasma accelerators. Consequently, this study may influence the design of future laser-based particle accelerators. To facilitate broader application, the response drag and associated radiation formulas are expected to be implemented in Geant4. The authors anticipate that this research will inspire further investigations into similar phenomena within various medium types. Finally, the authors acknowledge that the response drag phenomenon was initially identified by one of the co-authors, Dr. A. K. Azimov, during his undergraduate studies. Dr. Azimov's early insight into this phenomenon has been instrumental in advancing the field of particle transport in conductive media. This paper introduces a statistical approach to the Closest Neighbor Classification algorithm, specifically addressing imbalanced datasets. The proposed method relies on the assumption that data within each class adheres to a multivariate normal distribution. By utilizing the multivariate normal distribution function, the study calculates the likelihood of each data point belonging to a specific class based on its class means and covariance matrices. Consequently, classification is determined by assigning the point to the class with the highest probability. The authors present a proof for this method and demonstrate its effectiveness through a numerical example. Furthermore, the paper compares the outcomes of this proposed approach against those generated by the standard Closest Neighbor algorithm. Finally, the study concludes by outlining the method's advantages and potential areas for future research. Keywords: Classification, Multivariate Normal Distribution, Imbalanced Data, Closest Neighbor Algorithm.

Utilizing the SkyMapper Southern Survey, we have identified 1,000 new quasars, bringing the total count of known quasars to 14,000. This study focuses on the 100 brightest objects from this discovery, which are situated at redshifts exceeding 2.5. We present the luminosity function for quasars at $z>2.5$ across the $i'$-band magnitude range of 13.5 to 17.5. Our findings indicate that the luminosity function flattens at the bright end, a trend that aligns with the observed flattening of the number count slope. We estimate the rate density of these ultra-bright quasars to be approximately $10^{-5}$ Mpc$^{-3}$ Gyr$^{-1}$, a value that is notably higher than previous estimates. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the luminosity function of quasars at $z>2.5$ can be described by a double power-law model, where the break luminosity is determined by the $i'$-band magnitude. This analysis reveals a distinct break in the luminosity function at $M_{i'}=-26.5$, marking the transition point where the population shifts from bright to ultra-bright quasars. We also provide a detailed analysis of the brightest quasar, SDSS J1030+0524, which exhibits a bolometric luminosity of $10^{47.2}$ erg s$^{-1}$, a black hole mass of $10^{10.0}$ solar masses, and an accretion rate of $10^{-1.0}$ Eddington. Finally, we discuss the implications of these ultra-bright quasars for the evolution of the luminosity function and the growth of supermassive black holes. This study introduces contraction conditions applicable to admissible solutions of systems of conservation laws, specifically targeting discontinuities that adhere to the Rankine-Hugoniot conditions. These laws govern various physical phenomena, including fluid dynamics, elasticity, and heat transfer. The proposed contraction criteria are formulated using entropy functions that remain convex and differentiable across the entire state space. The analysis demonstrates that these conditions are satisfied by several prominent contraction frameworks, notably those built upon the Kruzkov entropy and the Entropy-Varentsov entropy-dissipation rate. Furthermore, the paper establishes that these contraction properties facilitate the derivation of $C^1$-norm estimates for convex differentiable functions evaluated at admissible solutions. This finding extends the classical framework of contraction metrics, which are traditionally defined on the tangent spaces of the solution set for hyperbolic systems of conservation laws. The results are applicable to various well-known contraction metrics, including those constructed from the Kruzkov entropy and the Entropy-Varentsov entropy-dissipation rate. Additionally, the study offers a novel approach to defining contraction metrics for the specific case of $2\times2$ systems of conservation laws. The paper concludes with illustrative examples, such as the Euler equations for ideal gases and the shallow water equations. The findings are anticipated to have significant implications for the theory of conservation laws, particularly in addressing the longstanding open problem of whether contraction metrics exist for general frameworks of conservation laws. This inquiry was originally proposed by A. Kuznetsov in his 1993 survey on the mathematical theory of conservation laws. The existence of such metrics would enable the extension of the contraction mapping principle to the space of admissible solutions, thereby providing a constructive method for solving systems of conservation laws. This would represent a substantial advancement over the current non-constructive existence theorems, which rely on the Leray-Schauder fixed point theorem. Ultimately, these findings could pave the way for the development of efficient numerical methods for conservation laws, grounded in the contraction mapping principle. This would mark a significant shift from the prevailing reliance on the Lax-Milgram theorem, which currently underpins most existing numerical methods. The proposed approach would also enable the application of the contraction mapping principle to the space of admissible solutions, a concept that has not yet been fully explored in the literature. This work aims to contribute to the ongoing effort to resolve the open problem of finding contraction metrics for frameworks of conservation laws, a task that has remained unsolved since Kuznetsov's survey. Perpetual view generation (PPG) involves creating multiple views from a single input image, a task that has recently leveraged conditional diffusion systems (CDS) to achieve high-fidelity, high-diversity, and view-consistent results. However, CDS methods often suffer from unreliable CDS conditioning, leading to degraded image quality, reduced diversity, and inconsistent geometry. To address these challenges, we introduce DiffDreamer, a novel framework designed for high-quality, high-diversity, and view-consistent PPG. Our approach employs a two-stage strategy: first, a 3D-consistent image generator produces a set of high-quality, view-consistent images based on the input; second, a CDS-based image-to-image translation model maps these generated images to the target viewpoints. We also propose a two-step training protocol that pre-trains the image generator and subsequently trains the image-to-image model using a carefully curated synthetic dataset. Extensive experiments across three real-world benchmarks demonstrate that DiffDreamer significantly outperforms existing methods in both qualitative and quantitative metrics. This paper introduces a data-driven framework designed to predict, improve, and control networked processes. The approach relies on a network representation where nodes signify the process states and edges denote their interconnections. Initially, a graph neural network is trained to learn the interactions between nodes and state transitions, enabling process prediction. Subsequently, a graph-based reward function is developed to evaluate various control strategies. Finally, a graph-based reinforcement learning algorithm is employed to derive an optimal control policy that maximizes this reward. The proposed method is applied to the Susceptible-Infected-Susceptible (SIS) epidemic model, demonstrating its efficacy in mitigating disease spread. Numerical simulations confirm that the approach successfully predicts the SIS epidemic's evolution and optimally controls infection propagation on networks. Furthermore, the study reveals that the model's performance is robust across different graph topologies and remains consistent even when initial conditions are inaccurate. The entire framework is implemented using Python and PyTorch, with all code available on GitHub. The Python package PyNet is also introduced to facilitate the application of this methodology. The paper concludes by outlining potential extensions and future research directions.

Keywords: data-driven, prediction, control, network, graph neural network, reinforcement learning, Python, PyTorch, epidemic, SIS model.

This study examines the Rayleigh-Plateau instability affecting a liquid layer coating a cylindrical fibre, incorporating both surface tension and slip-augmented viscous dissipation within the bulk fluid. By utilizing a perturbation method, we derive the dispersion relation for the system. Our findings indicate that slip can either accelerate or decelerate the growth rate of the instability, contingent upon the specific parameters. Furthermore, we demonstrate that slip can trigger the onset of instability even when surface tension alone would result in a stable configuration. Finally, we validate these theoretical predictions through direct numerical simulations. The proposed model is applicable to scenarios such as liquid bridges formed between two fibres or within the capillaries of a fibre bundle. Additionally, we explore the potential for generating non-axisymmetric instabilities in a liquid layer surrounding a rotating fibre. These insights could be valuable for advancing technologies in fibre coating and liquid transport. Finally, we outline the necessary modifications to adapt this model for analyzing the Rayleigh-Plateau instability in a liquid layer on a cylinder subjected to external pressure. These adjustments are also pertinent for investigating the instability of liquid bridges between two spheres. Ultimately, this research contributes to a deeper understanding of the physics governing liquid bridges and liquid coating processes. We demonstrate the Lipschitz stability of the hypersurface defined by horizontal differentials under the Riemannian metric of the frame bundle, thereby establishing Lipschitz stability for the Hunter-Saxton formula. This outcome relies on a geometric characterization of solenoidal vector fields through Riemannian curvature components and utilizes the regularity properties of the Monge-Ampère equation. **Background:** Scoliosis is a common condition characterized by spinal curvature, which can be assessed using ultrasound. However, the accuracy of this method depends heavily on the operator's skill. This study aimed to evaluate the reliability of ultrasound imaging for scoliosis when performed by a robot compared to manual scanning by a human.

**Methods:** Scoliosis was simulated on a spine phantom using a 3D-printed model. Ultrasound scans were acquired from the right side of the phantom using both robotic and manual ultrasound systems. The robotic system employed a 3D ultrasound probe mounted on a 6-degree-of-frontom (6DoF) manipulator, controlled via a probe trajectory plan generated by a scoliosis estimation algorithm. Scoliosis angles were calculated using the Cobb angle method. The ultrasound data were analyzed using the ultrasound-based scoliosis estimation algorithm, which utilizes a deep learning model to reconstruct 3D ultrasound volumes from 2D slices.

**Results:** The results indicated that robotic ultrasound imaging is more reliable than manual scanning. Specifically, the mean absolute error for scoliosis angle estimation was 1.8 degrees with robotic imaging versus 3.5 degrees with manual scanning. Additionally, the standard deviation for robotic imaging was 1.1 degrees, compared to 2.4 degrees for manual scanning.

**Conclusion:** These findings suggest that robot-assisted ultrasound imaging offers a more reliable approach to scoliosis evaluation than manual scanning. This enhanced reliability is attributed to the robot's ability to consistently execute the optimal scanning trajectory. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that scoliosis can be accurately estimated using ultrasound, a modality that is less invasive and more cost-effective than traditional CT or X-ray methods. The proposed ultrasound-based scoliosis estimation algorithm is applicable to both robotic and manual imaging.

**Significance:** This research highlights the potential of robot-assisted ultrasound for scoliosis assessment, offering a more reliable diagnostic tool than conventional imaging techniques. The proposed ultrasound-based scoliosis estimation algorithm is versatile and can be utilized with both robotic and manual ultrasound systems. Ultimately, robot-assisted ultrasound imaging provides a more effective solution for scoliosis evaluation than standard manual techniques. Future work will focus on validating these results using ultrasound data from human subjects.

**Keywords:** Scoliosis, Ultrasound, Robot-assisted Ultrasound, Deep Learning, 3D Ultrasound Reconstruction.

This study introduces a novel, non-statistical approach for generating a collection of speech utterances with varying lengths based on a single median-length source. The method operates by repeatedly applying a combination of stretching and shrinking transformations to the source until a predetermined number of utterances is reached. The parameters governing these transformations are derived from the statistical analysis of a group of human speakers. The paper details the procedure, outlines the necessary assumptions, and presents experimental results. These findings demonstrate that the proposed method successfully produces utterances with diverse lengths while effectively preserving the original speaker identity. Furthermore, the method achieves a higher success rate in retaining speaker identity compared to a method previously suggested by the authors. The research concludes that the non-statistical approach is viable for creating synthetic utterances of multiple lengths from a single source, making it particularly suitable for applications where a limited number of real utterances are available. Additionally, the method is applicable to any type of audio, including music and natural sounds. Future work will explore the method's effectiveness in simulating a wide range of human speaker ages. This study introduces a multidimensional framework for analyzing multiple time-to-event data, with a specific focus on time-to-recovery trajectories. The approach employs a piecewise linear model to estimate latent health states, which are defined as segments of these trajectories. These states are inferred using a multiple state examination model, a method that offers a novel perspective on longitudinal data by modeling the hazard of transitioning between health states. The analysis incorporates time-varying covariates to examine how both time and individual characteristics influence health trajectories. The proposed methodology is applied to a dataset of patients who experienced myocardial infarction, with the objective of identifying distinct life course health pathways. The results highlight the existence of two primary pathways: one characterized by a gradual return to health, and another by a sudden decline in health status. Furthermore, the study investigates how lifestyle factors and comorbidities influence these pathways. The methodology is implemented within the R statistical software, with code available at https://github.com/JulieBoussageau/MSE. The R package, named "MSE," can be installed via the command "devtools::install_github('JulieBoussageau/MSE')". The package is structured into three main components: (i) the MSE model, (ii) the transition model, and (iii) the health trajectory model. Additionally, the package includes a function to generate visualizations of the estimated trajectories. The authors acknowledge that the model's performance may be limited when applied to short time intervals. We introduce a quadrature technique for evaluating the molecular continuum of one-electron atoms and ions using a multi-site basis approach. This process involves solving a system of linear equations derived from a quadrature of a non-local integral operator, followed by a correction step that eliminates quadrature errors. The method is applied to hydrogen-like ions across a broad spectrum of nuclear charges, demonstrating that it achieves high accuracy with a relatively small basis set. Furthermore, we present results regarding the energy levels of helium and lithium. The approach relies on the development of a novel correction method, which we believe will be applicable to other quadrature problems. Additionally, we have created an open-source Python package, `continuum`, to facilitate the application of this technique. This includes a collection of pre-computed, open-access tables for hydrogen-like ions spanning nuclear charges from $Z=1$ to $Z=118$. These tables contain data on binding energies, quantum defects, and the energies of the $1s$ and $2s$ thresholds. Our findings indicate that quantum defects vary smoothly with nuclear charge, a result that aligns with the recent discovery of a universal Rydberg series in hydrogen-like argon. We also provide the $1s$ binding energies for hydrogen-like ions as a function of nuclear charge. Finally, we discuss the potential for extending this quadrature method to other continuum problems. A set of vertices $S$ in a graph $G$ constitutes a resolving set if the distance vectors from every vertex in $G$ to the vertices in $S$ are unique. The metric dimension of $G$, denoted $\beta(G)$, is the smallest possible size of such a resolving set. This paper examines the metric dimension as a parameter within the framework of parameterized complexity. We demonstrate that the Metric Dimension problem is fixed-parameter tractable (FPT) when parameterized by the size of a feedback vertex set, the vertex cover number, and the path cover number. Furthermore, we establish that Metric Dimension remains FPT when parameterized by the distance to an interval graph, the distance to a cocomparability graph, and the pruned clique-width. Finally, we introduce a kernelization algorithm that reduces any input instance to a kernel of size $O(k^3)$, where $k$ represents the feedback vertex set number. These findings are derived by leveraging the relationship between metric dimension and the dimension of the associated geometric graph. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive survey of existing algorithms and results regarding metric dimension in the context of parameterized complexity.

This study examines the potential for abrupt, recurring climate shifts in Earth-like atmospheres characterized by elevated greenhouse gas levels. We introduce a straightforward model that captures the core dynamics of such climate systems, which are governed by a nonlinear interaction between atmospheric heating and surface cooling. Our findings indicate that the model's parameters align with those of actual planetary bodies, including Venus and the early Earth. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a simplified version of this model exhibits complex behavior, specifically period-doubling bifurcations leading to chaos. Crucially, we identify a novel mechanism for recurrent climate transitions driven by the interplay between period-doubling and period-halving bifurcations. This process generates a sequence of recurrent events with progressively shorter periods, a phenomenon we term "episodes." We illustrate how this results in a complex pattern of recurrent climate episodes and highlight its relevance to the recurrent flooding observed on Mars. Additionally, we explore the possibility that similar episodes could occur in early Earth's climate, potentially influencing the evolution of life. Finally, we discuss the broader implications of these results for understanding the behavior of current and future terrestrial climates. These findings underscore the necessity of developing a more comprehensive model that accounts for recurrent climate episodes. To achieve this, we propose a framework for analyzing bifurcations in climate models that are driven by the saturation of radiative heating. This is especially pertinent to the search for biosignatures, as recurrent events could mask or mimic biological signals. We introduce a twistor action that extends the self-dual Yang-Mills equations to include Yang-Mills extensions of the higher-spin extensions of (anti-)self-dual Yang-Mills equations in four dimensions. This framework relies on a novel class of differential operators, termed \textit{twistor creations}, which operate on fields dependent on the twistor line. We demonstrate that the resulting equations of motion correspond precisely to the higher-spin self-dual Yang-Mills equations. Additionally, we explore a twistor extension of the full Yang-Mills equations and provide an explicit action for five-dimensional self-dual Yang-Mills theory. A key distinction between our approach and the original twistor action for higher-spin Yang-Mills lies in the fact that our twistor fields exhibit no dependence on extra twistor coordinates. Furthermore, we establish that our twistor action remains invariant under a continuous deformation of its twistor dependence, a feature that facilitates the derivation of the higher-spin self-dual Yang-Mills equations. Finally, we examine the implications of our findings for the amplitudes associated with higher-spin self-dual Yang-Mills theories. Medical image datasets are frequently plagued by label noise, a challenge that Bayesian statistics offer a solution to. This study introduces the Statistics Directed Label Renovation Mechanism (SLRM), which utilizes a Bayesian framework to mitigate noisy labels in medical image classification tasks. The mechanism operates in two stages: first, it calculates the probability distribution of each image to identify the most probable class; second, it reassigns the image to this most probable class. We evaluated SLRM across three medical image datasets—ISIC2018, HAM10000, and Kvasir-1000—employing ResNet50 as the base model. The findings demonstrate that applying SLRM enhances classification accuracy by 1.5%, 2.5%, and 2.5% for the respective datasets. Furthermore, we analyzed the impact of varying prior distributions on SLRM, observing that a uniform prior distribution yields superior performance. These results indicate that SLRM is effective in reducing label noise within medical image classification datasets. This paper aims to demonstrate that for $p>1$, the norm of the Lagrange interpolation operator at the nodes $\{x_{n,k}\}_{k=0}^n$ within the space $W_{p}^{(r)}[0,1]$ is bounded by $Cn^{r-1/p'}$, where $C$ is a constant independent of $n$, $p$, and $r$. This result extends the findings of V. A. Popov [1] and R. DeVore and V. A. Popov [2]. Additionally, we establish that for $p=1$, the bound becomes $Cn^r$. Furthermore, we show that for $p>1$, the bound for the norm of the Lagrange interpolation operator at the nodes $\{t_{n,k}\}_{k=0}^n$ in the space $W_{p}^{(r)}[0,1]$ is also $Cn^{r-1/p'}$. The proof relies on the discrete Hilbert transform and its properties. Finally, we derive that the norm of the Lagrange interpolation operator at the nodes $\{t_{n,k}\}_{k=0}^n$ in the space $L_{p}[0,1]$ is bounded by $Cn^{1/p'}$.

Additionally, the methodologies and conclusions in this study can be applied to investigate various graph polynomials and their corresponding properties. Finally, we outline several potential directions for future research.

This study introduces a data-informed approach to enhance the predictive capabilities of coherent structure-based models for instantaneous wall turbulence. By employing a low-order data-driven model to capture the dynamics of a canonical wall-bounded turbulent flow, we identify discrepancies between these data models and established physics-based models. These differences guide the development of an improved physics-based model that aligns more closely with data predictions. The resulting data-informed physics-based model demonstrates superior performance in forecasting both instantaneous and time-averaged statistics compared to the original physics-based model. Furthermore, this methodology is applicable to other low-dimensional models and can be utilized to refine physics-based models for various turbulent flows. The experimental validation of the Anomalous Screening Theory (AST) within a geotechnical centrifuge demonstrates that both the screening effect and the resulting linear stress-strain relationship in dense granular assemblies are fundamentally driven by the agglomeration of inter-particle frictional contacts. This phenomenon is characterized by a reduced effective coordination number, which scales with the square root of the applied strain. Furthermore, the study confirms the universal nature of AST across various particle sizes and materials, including both frictional and frictionless systems. These findings provide a unified theoretical framework for explaining the diverse mechanical behaviors observed in dense granular media. Granular materials are ubiquitous in both natural and engineered environments, exhibiting a wide range of mechanical behaviors. Their unique properties stem from the complex interactions between individual particles, which are governed by the balance between frictional and non-frictional forces. This balance is influenced by particle shape, size distribution, and material composition. The intricate nature of these interactions gives rise to a variety of mechanical phenomena, such as the formation of force chains, the development of shear bands, and the emergence of non-linear stress-strain relationships. In this study, we focus on the latter phenomenon, specifically the non-linear stress-strain relationship observed in dense granular assemblies. This behavior is characterized by a linear increase in stress with strain at small deformations, followed by a deviation from linearity at larger strains. This transition marks the onset of plastic deformation and is accompanied by a reduction in the coordination number, representing the average number of contacts per particle. The objective of this work is to provide a comprehensive explanation for this phenomenon by integrating experimental data with theoretical modeling. To achieve this, we employ the Anomalous Screening Theory (AST), a recently developed framework that posits the agglomeration of frictional contacts as the primary mechanism driving the non-linear stress-strain relationship. By combining AST with a universal scaling law for the coordination number, we can accurately predict the stress-strain relationship in dense granular assemblies. Sgr A East, a supernova remnant situated near the Galactic center, is hypothesized to be the result of a stellar explosion that occurred approximately 2.5 million years ago. The progenitor of this explosion remains unidentified, with two primary hypotheses: it was either a massive star that evolved rapidly and died shortly before the explosion, or a lower-mass star that underwent significant mass accretion from a binary companion over a longer timescale. This study utilizes a Monte Carlo simulation to evaluate the likelihood of the latter scenario by modeling the dynamical evolution of massive binary systems. Our findings indicate that the explosion likely originated from a star with an initial mass between 15 and 20 solar masses, which accreted a substantial amount of mass from its companion. Furthermore, the explosion probably took place within a distance of 0.1 to 0.2 parsecs from the Galactic center. These results offer a more precise understanding of the explosion's origin and its impact on the surrounding environment. Additionally, we propose that the star responsible for the explosion may have been the progenitor of the radio source Sgr A West. Finally, we discuss the implications of this explosion for the formation of the central black hole. This research was conducted using the Galaxy Evolution Code (GalEv). Multi-class text categorization is a fundamental Natural Language Processing (NLP) task that has gained significant attention in recent years. A primary challenge in this domain is class imbalance, where the majority class dominates, often resulting in models that fail to effectively learn minority classes. To address this, various data-level and algorithm-level techniques have been developed. This study focuses on data-level approaches, specifically comparing three methods: SMOTE, SMOTE-MB, and SMOTE-MB*. Our work introduces a novel method, SMOTE-MB*, which demonstrates superior performance in classifying minority classes compared to the others. We evaluated these techniques across three datasets with varying numbers of classes, utilizing three distinct machine learning algorithms. Our findings indicate that while no single approach is optimal across all scenarios, SMOTE-MB* consistently outperforms the others in terms of accuracy. Additionally, we observed that the performance of these methods is more sensitive to the number of classes than to the specific algorithm used. Finally, we conducted a detailed analysis of the generated synthetic samples to provide deeper insights into the characteristics of the imbalanced datasets. This study examines the interrelationships between regional news coverage, COVID-19 metrics (cases, fatalities, vaccination rates), and audience demographics within the United States. Utilizing data from the News Data Consortium, the study analyzes over 1.5 million news articles published between March and December 2020, alongside corresponding audience statistics. By applying a multivariate regression model, the research identifies correlations between coverage volume and COVID-19 data, as well as variations in coverage across different audience groups. The findings indicate that, on average, regions with higher case counts received more extensive news coverage, while coverage of COVID-19 specifically was more prevalent in areas with lower death rates. Furthermore, the study observed that coverage was disproportionately directed toward regions with higher proportions of White residents and individuals aged 25 to 44. These results offer valuable insights for news organizations aiming to refine their reporting strategies and for policymakers seeking to understand how media coverage influences public perception. Additionally, the research underscores the necessity for further investigation into the causal relationships between news coverage and audience demographics. The preservation of physical conservation laws is a critical requirement for any computational method used in physics simulations. This study examines the accuracy of angular momentum preservation within the rapid multipole method (RMM) for solving the Poisson equation. We demonstrate that the discrete set of RMM grid points inherently forms a set of spherical shells, which facilitates conservation. Furthermore, we establish that the error in total angular momentum within a cell scales as $O(h^2)$, where $h$ represents the cell size. These findings are supported by numerical simulations. Additionally, we present a technique to enhance RMM accuracy by constructing a higher-order multipole expansion for the Poisson equation, which reduces the angular momentum error to the order of the base RMM solution. Finally, we apply this improved approach to calculate the self-force experienced by a particle moving through a uniform background charge. In this context, the conservation of angular momentum serves as a valuable metric for evaluating the accuracy of the computed self-force. We demonstrate that this higher-order expansion significantly boosts RMM precision, reducing the relative error in angular momentum from $10^{-3}$ to $10^{-6}$. Consequently, the error in the self-force is reduced from $10^{-3}$ to $10^{-6}$. This enhancement is particularly beneficial for scenarios involving high angular momentum, such as a particle orbiting a black hole. In such cases, the relative error in the self-force can reach $10^{-1}$, a level that is often unacceptable for physics simulations. Our proposed method reduces this error to $10^{-6}$, thereby substantially improving the fidelity of the simulation results. This work was conducted in collaboration with the group of Prof. S. This study examines the shift in proton polarization within the elastic scattering process $e\vec{p} \to e\vec{p}$, a phenomenon that has garnered significant attention in recent years. We demonstrate that this shift is contingent upon the specific elastic form factors of the proton. Furthermore, we establish that the eponymous polarization shift can be quantified using a single dimensionless variable, $\xi$, which represents the ratio of the proton's transverse to longitudinal polarization. The final expression for the shift depends exclusively on $\xi$ and the elastic scattering form factors. Additionally, we analyze the potential of this shift to constrain the proton's electric and magnetic Sachs form factors, $G_E$ and $G_M$, across a broad range of momentum transfers. Our findings indicate that the proton's polarization can be determined with high precision, particularly at low values of $\xi$. This paper investigates K3 surfaces that admit a Siegel disk, with a primary focus on determining the possible Picard values. We demonstrate the existence of such K3 surfaces with a Siegel disk of any prescribed Kodaira-Spitzer type, achieving this by calculating the necessary Picard values. Furthermore, we establish that the set of feasible Picard values forms a countable set. Our approach relies heavily on the theory of Siegel disks within K3 surfaces, as well as on the concepts of heights and the distribution of algebraic points on moduli spaces. Additionally, we examine K3 surfaces featuring an isolated fixed point, deriving several results that may hold independent significance. Finally, we explore the relationship between the heights of moduli points and the orders of non-tangency of these points. This connection is instrumental in proving that the heights of moduli points associated with K3 surfaces possessing Siegel disks grow without bound. As a consequence, we derive an upper bound for the orders of non-tangency, which serves as a key component in our analysis. The methodology employed here is also applicable to other moduli problems. We investigate a dark matter scenario involving a nearly mass-degenerate neutralino with mixed gaugino and higgsino components. This dark matter candidate is stable on cosmological timescales due to a discrete $Z_2$ symmetry, but it can decay over longer periods through a small, explicitly broken $R$-parity. The primary decay mechanism is a two-loop process mediated by a virtual charged lepton, which is suppressed by the mass gap between the dark matter and its decay products. This suppression ensures that the dark matter's contribution to the dark radiation density ($\Delta N_{\rm eff}$) remains within the limits set by Planck data. The gamma-ray spectrum resulting from the decay of these dark matter particles in the early universe exhibits a quasi-monochromatic peak. This signal could be detectable by the upcoming CTA observatory if the dark matter mass is approximately 100 GeV. Additionally, we examine the potential for detecting this signal through dark matter decay occurring in the present day. In this case, the gamma-ray spectrum would show a broadened peak, and its intensity would be directly proportional to the local dark matter density. We find that this scenario is viable for dark matter masses up to roughly 100 GeV. Furthermore, we explore the possibility of a secondary peak in the gamma-ray spectrum, which would arise from the decay of the primary daughter particles produced in the initial neutralino decay. This secondary peak is also accessible to CTA for masses below 100 GeV. Finally, we analyze the parameter space of this model and discuss its implications for the muon $g-2$ anomaly. Our findings indicate that this framework offers a promising avenue for explaining the muon $g-2$ discrepancy. Specifically, the required parameter values to address the $g-2$ anomaly fall within the region favored by CTA. Consequently, this model provides a unified explanation for both the muon $g-2$ anomaly and the dark matter density. Furthermore, the parameter space required to explain the muon $g-2$ is consistent with the dark radiation constraints derived from Planck data. This suggests that the gamma-ray signal from dark matter decay is likely to be observable in the near future. Finally, we outline the future prospects of this model. If the gamma-ray signal from dark matter decay is detected, it would confirm the existence of a new light force carrier, thereby violating $R$-parity and offering a solution to the muon $g-2$ problem.

The genus of a graph, defined as the minimum number of handles required for a torus to accommodate a specific graph embedding on a surface topologically equivalent to that shaped torus, has been a subject of interest for mathematicians and computer scientists. While the most straightforward approach to determine the genus of a graph $G$ involves enumerating all possible embeddings and identifying the one with the fewest handles, this brute-force method is impractical for graphs with a large number of vertices. This study introduces an efficient algorithm that approximates the genus of a dense graph within a factor of 2. The proposed method relies on a novel technique for estimating the genus of dense graphs by analyzing the cycle rank of their cycle matroids. This technique leverages the observation that the cycle rank of a dense graph's cycle matroid closely approximates the genus of the graph itself. We demonstrate that the genus of a dense graph can be calculated within a factor of 2 in polynomial time by solving a system of linear equations over a finite field. Furthermore, we establish that this algorithm achieves an approximation ratio of $O(\log n)$ for sparse graphs. Consequently, we conclude that the genus of any graph can be estimated within a factor of $O(\log n)$ in polynomial time. These findings are supported by experimental results. The proposed method enables the rapid estimation of the genus for dense graphs, a capability that was previously unattainable. Additionally, the algorithm is applicable to sparse graphs, offering a significant advancement in graph theory. The method is particularly valuable for graph theorists, as it provides a means to estimate the genus of a graph without requiring the enumeration of all possible embeddings. This paper presents a comprehensive overview of the algorithm, its theoretical underpinnings, and its applications. This paper introduces a randomized Newton approach for convex optimization within a multi-agent framework. In this setup, $n$ agents collaborate to minimize a sum of individual functions, where each agent possesses knowledge of only its own function. The proposed algorithm operates in two stages: first, agents conduct a distributed computation to approximate the gradient of their collective function at a shared point; second, they execute a distributed descent using these approximations. The method is applicable to both differentiable and non-differentiable functions. For differentiable cases, the algorithm achieves linear convergence, whereas for non-differentiable functions, it converges sublinearly. Furthermore, the analysis demonstrates that the computational burden per agent remains constant, independent of the number of agents. Experimental results confirm the method's efficacy in solving distributed convex problems. Additionally, the algorithm is robust to a subset of agents being inactive during specific iterations. Finally, the paper extends this approach to address distributed constrained optimization. The theoretical findings are supported by numerical experiments. This research examines the efficacy of transfer learning in identifying hate speech within Hindi and Bengali languages. Time projection chambers (TPCs) utilizing gas detectors offer exceptional spatial and temporal resolution, making them ideal for measuring nuclear recoil energies in dark matter experiments. However, the finite energy resolution of gas detectors restricts the observability of light dark matter recoils. To address this, TPCs must employ novel detector gases and technologies capable of measuring recoil energies with a resolution of a few eV. This paper outlines the design of such a TPC and introduces new observables designed to enhance the detection of low-energy nuclear recoils. Specifically, we examine the impact of these new observables on the sensitivity to dark matter nuclear recoils for a benchmark TPC configuration. Our findings indicate that the proposed observables can improve the nuclear recoil search sensitivity by up to an order of magnitude. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these observables are broadly applicable to any detector technology capable of resolving nuclear recoil energies at the few-eV scale. Finally, we discuss the potential for these observables to aid in distinguishing between nuclear and electronic recoil events. These advancements will significantly advance the prospects for detecting dark matter through nuclear recoil searches. We introduce a novel approach for identifying geodesic trajectories within Gaussian random field manifolds. This technique relies on a specific parametrization of geodesic paths, which is derived from a discrete approximation of geodesic equations. We demonstrate that this discrete formulation converges to the continuous form in the limit of a large number of discrete points. The proposed method is validated through two case studies: determining geodesic paths in a random field manifold representing a discretized 2D Euclidean space, and calculating geodesics between two 2D ellipsoids embedded within a 3D Euclidean space. Furthermore, we show that the geodesic distances generated by our algorithm align with those produced by the Riemannian distance metric. These findings indicate that the algorithm is effective for identifying trajectories in stochastic field manifolds. Additionally, we observe that the computational cost of this algorithm scales linearly with the number of points used for parametrization. Finally, we demonstrate that the algorithm's performance remains robust even when the underlying stochastic field exhibits strong non-Gaussianity. These results suggest that the proposed method is applicable to a broad range of stochastic field models. The algorithm is implemented in Python and is publicly accessible. We develop a length-count formula for a hyperbolic surface with conical singularities that features a set of geodesic length constraints. This formulation serves as a non-abelian analogue to the Delsarte-type trace formula applicable to Poincaré surfaces. By applying this formula, we derive an explicit expression for the periodic length function, which counts geodesics on a surface of revolution that wind around the cylinder exactly once. This specific instance of the periodic length function had previously been conjectured by Gourevitch and Zudilin. Furthermore, we establish a functional equation for this function, which yields a novel identity for the q-Pochhammer symbol. Finally, we provide a detailed analysis of the asymptotic behavior of the periodic length function, demonstrating that it exhibits log-periodic oscillations. This behavior arises from the presence of a Siegel zero, a phenomenon that parallels the logarithmic growth observed in the number of perfect squares. Additionally, we offer a new perspective on the distribution of quadratic residues and non-residues modulo p. This paper establishes the arithmetic and analytic properties of meromorphic functions arising as factors of the L-functions for modular patterns. Specifically, we demonstrate that these factors are both single-valued and algebraically independent over the field of modular functions. Our primary finding is that the Nevanlinna characteristics of these factors remain bounded. This result extends the boundedness of the growth order for factors previously proven by the second author in [J. Number Theory 130 (2010), 1003-1020]. Furthermore, our results provide the first proof of the boundedness of the error term in the asymptotic expansion of the counting function for algebraic points on the Siegel Nevanlinna function, thereby confirming a conjecture by the first author [Compositio Math. 146 (2010), 1003-1018]. As an additional application, we derive a novel characterization of the set of Hecke characters associated with abelian extensions of totally real fields, expressed through the analytic properties of the corresponding L-functions. Finally, we offer an alternative proof of the analytic class number formula for totally real abelian extensions utilizing the analytic properties of these factors. The methodology employed relies on the theory of Nevanlinna functions, the Shimura-Taniyama-Weil conjecture, the Langlands-Shahidi method, and the Rankin-Selberg method. Additionally, we establish a new approach to the analytic continuation of the L-functions for modular patterns, which is essential for the proof of our main theorem. This approach draws upon the work of Gross-Kohnen-Zagier, Gross-Zagier, and the authors of [Compositio Math. 146 (2010), 1003-1018]. The techniques utilized are anticipated to have broader applications in the investigation of the arithmetic and analytic properties of modular forms and their associated L-functions. Finally, we propose a conjecture regarding the analytic properties of these L-functions, inspired by the theorems presented in this study. We believe this conjecture holds significant potential for advancing the understanding of the analytic properties of L-functions within the framework of the Langlands program. A graph $G$ is defined as pancyclic if it contains cycles of every length $k$ for $3 \leq k \leq |V(G)|$. The autonomy number of a graph $G$, denoted $\alpha(G)$, represents the smallest integer $k$ such that $G$ possesses a spanning subgraph with autonomy number $k$. This paper establishes that for any pancyclic graph $G$ with autonomy number $k$, there exists a spanning subgraph with autonomy number at most $k+1$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this bound is tight by constructing an infinite family of pancyclic graphs where every member $G$ has autonomy number $k$, yet its minimum spanning autonomous subgraph requires an autonomy number of $k+1$. Additionally, we examine Hamiltonicity and autonomy number within the context of pan-acyclic graphs, proving that every Hamiltonian pan-acyclic graph $G$ admits a spanning subgraph with autonomy number at most $\alpha(G)+1$. We also present an infinite family of pan-acyclic graphs where the autonomy number of the minimum spanning autonomous subgraph exceeds $\alpha(G)$ by exactly one. Finally, we provide a characterization of the autonomy number for graphs possessing a Hamiltonian spanning tree. These findings are supported by a Python package, AutonomyNumber, which includes an algorithm to compute the autonomy number for graphs with a Hamiltonian spanning tree. The paper concludes with several open problems. The source code and associated data files can be accessed at https://github.com/autonomynumber. This study introduces a new approach to solving the time-independent Schrödinger equation for atoms and molecules subjected to strong direct current (DC) fields. By applying complex scaling to the radial coordinate outward from the origin, we derive outward complex scaled Hamiltonians. These Hamiltonians yield eigenvalues that correspond to the energy eigenvalues of the original unscaled Hamiltonian. The research demonstrates that outward complex scaling remains effective for systems with high charge, including atoms and molecules. Furthermore, it is shown that this technique successfully handles eigenstates within the continuous spectrum of the DC-field Hamiltonian, which are typically difficult to treat. The study confirms that eigenvalues and eigenstates can be computed for atoms and molecules across a broad range of DC-field strengths. Additionally, the paper examines the impact of the complex scaling angle on the solutions of the DC-field Hamiltonian. Finally, the out-of-the-box (OTB) outward complex scaled Hamiltonian is utilized to calculate the AC Stark shift and the Autler-Townes effect in atoms and molecules under strong alternating current (AC) fields. These findings indicate that the OTB method remains valid for atoms and molecules exposed to strong AC fields. The paper concludes by discussing the future applications of this approach.
